lessons.title: Getting Started with Excel and Google Sheets
lessons.summary: You will be able to find your way around Excel and Google Sheets, enter and edit data, work with rows, columns and sheets, and save files in the right format.
goals: Name the main parts of the Excel and Google Sheets window (ribbon/menus, Name Box, formula bar, sheet tabs)
Read and write cell addresses and ranges such as C4 and A1:C5
Enter, edit and delete data and select cells, rows, columns and ranges
Insert and delete rows and columns, and add, rename and move sheets
Save a workbook as .xlsx or .csv and open an .xlsx file in Google Sheets
Use keyboard shortcuts to move quickly around a large table
lessons.theory:
A spreadsheet is a program that stores information in a big table and can calculate with it. People use spreadsheets every day at work: shops track sales, teachers keep grades, accountants plan budgets, and managers make reports. In this course you will learn the two most popular spreadsheet programs: **Microsoft Excel** and **Google Sheets**. If you know one of them well, you can quickly learn the other.

## What can a spreadsheet do?

A spreadsheet can:

- keep lists (students, products, contacts, orders);
- calculate totals, averages and percentages automatically;
- sort and filter data to find answers quickly;
- show data as charts;
- update all results when you change one number.

For example, a small shop owner in Karaganda can type every sale into a spreadsheet. At the end of the month the spreadsheet shows the total sales without a calculator.

## The building blocks

| Term | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Workbook | The whole file. It contains one or more sheets. | `shop_2025.xlsx` |
| Sheet (worksheet) | One page (one table) inside the workbook. | `January`, `February` |
| Column | A vertical line of cells. Columns have letters. | A, B, C … Z, AA, AB … |
| Row | A horizontal line of cells. Rows have numbers. | 1, 2, 3 … |
| Cell | The box where one column and one row meet. | `B3` |
| Range | A rectangle of several cells. | `A1:C5` |

### Cell addresses

Every cell has an **address**: first the column letter, then the row number. The cell in column C and row 4 is `C4`. We never write the number first (`4C` is wrong).

A **range** is written with a colon between the top-left cell and the bottom-right cell. `A1:C5` means all cells from A1 to C5: 3 columns × 5 rows = 15 cells.

**Worked example 1.** Look at this small table:

|   | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Name | City | Age |
| 2 | Aidana Seitkali | Almaty | 18 |
| 3 | Nursultan Abenov | Astana | 19 |

- The word `City` is in cell `B1`.
- The number `19` is in cell `C3`.
- The range `A2:C3` contains 2 rows × 3 columns = **6 cells** (all the data about the two students).

> **Remember:** Column letter first, then row number: `B1`, not `1B`.

## The screen: Excel vs Google Sheets

Both programs look similar. The main parts are:

1. **Grid** – the cells, with column letters at the top and row numbers on the left.
2. **Active cell** – the selected cell. It has a thick border.
3. **Name Box** – a small box on the left above the grid. It shows the address of the active cell. You can also type an address there (for example `D150`) and press **Enter** to jump to that cell.
4. **Formula bar** – the long box next to the Name Box. It shows the real content of the active cell. Later you will type formulas here.
5. **Sheet tabs** – at the bottom. Click a tab to open another sheet.

| Part | Microsoft Excel | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|
| Commands | **Ribbon** with tabs: Home, Insert, Formulas, Data … | **Menus**: File, Edit, View, Insert, Format, Data … and a toolbar |
| Name Box | Left of the formula bar | Left of the formula bar |
| Formula bar | Marked with *fx* | Marked with *fx* |
| Add a sheet | **+** button next to the tabs | **+** button at the bottom left |
| Saving | You save (Ctrl+S), or AutoSave in OneDrive | Saves **automatically** to Google Drive |
| Where the file lives | On your computer or OneDrive | In Google Drive (online) |

## Entering, editing and deleting data

### Entering data

1. Click a cell.
2. Type a value (a word or a number).
3. Press **Enter** to move down, or **Tab** to move right.

### Editing data

- To **replace** the content: click the cell and just type. The old content disappears.
- To **change part** of the content: double-click the cell, or press **F2**, or click in the formula bar. Then move the cursor and fix the text. Press **Enter** to finish.
- Press **Esc** to cancel typing and keep the old value.

### Deleting data

- Select the cell or range and press **Delete**. This clears the **contents**, but the cell stays in its place.
- **Ctrl+Z** undoes your last action. **Ctrl+Y** redoes it.

> **Warning:** Pressing Delete clears the contents only. Deleting a **row** or **column** removes the whole line, and the cells below or to the right move to fill the space.

## Selecting cells and ranges

| What to select | How |
|---|---|
| One cell | Click it |
| A range | Drag with the mouse, or click the first cell and **Shift+click** the last cell |
| A whole column | Click the column letter (or **Ctrl+Space**) |
| A whole row | Click the row number (or **Shift+Space**) |
| Cells that are not next to each other | Hold **Ctrl** and click |
| The whole table | **Ctrl+A** |

## Inserting and deleting rows and columns

**In Excel:**

1. Right-click a row number (for example `5`).
2. Choose **Insert** – a new empty row appears **above** row 5. Old row 5 becomes row 6.
3. To delete, right-click the row number and choose **Delete**.

Columns work in the same way: a new column is inserted to the **left** of the selected column.

**In Google Sheets:** right-click a row number and choose **Insert 1 row above** or **Insert 1 row below**. For columns: **Insert 1 column left** or **Insert 1 column right**. To delete, choose **Delete row** or **Delete column**.

**Worked example 2.** A list has `Bread` in A2, `Milk` in A3 and `Tea` in A4. You right-click row 3 and choose Insert (Excel). Now A3 is empty, `Milk` moves to **A4**, and `Tea` moves to **A5**. If you then delete row 2, everything moves up one row: A2 is empty, `Milk` goes to **A3**, `Tea` goes to **A4**.

## Working with sheets

- **Add a sheet:** click the **+** button near the sheet tabs.
- **Rename a sheet:** double-click the tab (Excel) or right-click the tab and choose **Rename** (both programs). Type the new name and press **Enter**.
- **Move a sheet:** drag the tab left or right.
- **Delete a sheet:** right-click the tab and choose **Delete**.

> **Tip:** Give sheets clear names like `Sales 2025` or `Students`. Names like `Sheet1` and `Sheet2` say nothing about the data.

## Saving and file formats

| Format | What it keeps | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| `.xlsx` | All sheets, formatting, formulas | The normal Excel format. Use it most of the time. |
| `.csv` | Only plain values from **one** sheet, no formatting | To move data between programs and websites |
| Google Sheets file | Everything, stored online | Working in a browser and sharing with others |

**In Excel:** **File > Save As**, choose a folder, type a name and choose the file type. **Ctrl+S** saves again. If the file is in OneDrive, **AutoSave** can be switched on.

**In Google Sheets:** there is no Save button. Every change is saved to Google Drive automatically. To get a file: **File > Download** and choose *Microsoft Excel (.xlsx)* or *Comma-separated values (.csv)*.

### Opening an .xlsx file in Google Sheets

1. Go to Google Drive and click **New > File upload**.
2. Choose the `.xlsx` file.
3. Double-click it in Drive. It opens in Google Sheets.
4. Optional: **File > Save as Google Sheets** to make a real Google Sheets copy.

In this course every practice task has a starter `.xlsx` file. Excel users open it directly. Google Sheets users upload it to Drive first.

> **Warning:** When you save as CSV, only the **active sheet** is saved, and all colours, borders and formulas are lost. Keep an `.xlsx` copy too.

## Essential navigation shortcuts

| Action | Excel (Windows) | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|
| Move to the edge of the data | Ctrl+Arrow | Ctrl+Arrow |
| Go to cell A1 | Ctrl+Home | Ctrl+Home |
| Go to the last used cell | Ctrl+End | Ctrl+End |
| Select to the edge of the data | Ctrl+Shift+Arrow | Ctrl+Shift+Arrow |
| Next / previous sheet | Ctrl+Page Down / Ctrl+Page Up | Ctrl+Shift+Page Down / Ctrl+Shift+Page Up |
| Edit the active cell | F2 | F2 or Enter |
| Undo / Redo | Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y | Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y |
| Save | Ctrl+S | Automatic |

On a Mac, use **Cmd** instead of **Ctrl** for most shortcuts (for example Cmd+Z to undo).

> **Tip:** With 10,000 rows, scrolling takes a long time. **Ctrl+Down** jumps to the last row of the data in one second.

## Summary

- A workbook is a file; it contains sheets; a sheet is a grid of rows and columns.
- A cell address is column letter + row number, for example `C4`. A range is written like `A1:C5`.
- The Name Box shows the address of the active cell and lets you jump to any cell.
- The formula bar shows the real content of a cell.
- Excel uses a ribbon; Google Sheets uses menus and a toolbar.
- Delete clears contents; deleting a row or column removes it and moves other cells.
- `.xlsx` keeps everything; `.csv` keeps only the values of one sheet.
- Google Sheets saves automatically; in Excel press Ctrl+S.

## Key terms

- **Workbook** — a spreadsheet file with one or more sheets.
- **Sheet (worksheet)** — one table inside a workbook.
- **Cell** — one box in the grid, where a row and a column meet.
- **Cell address** — the name of a cell, such as `B7`.
- **Range** — a rectangular group of cells, such as `A1:D10`.
- **Active cell** — the cell that is selected now.
- **Name Box** — the box that shows the active cell address.
- **Formula bar** — the box that shows the content of the active cell.
- **Ribbon** — the row of tabs and buttons at the top of Excel.
- **CSV** — a simple text file format with values separated by commas.

lessons.title: Data Types and Formatting
lessons.summary: You will be able to tell numbers, text and dates apart and format a table so it is clear, correct and professional.
goals: Recognise numbers, text and dates, and find numbers stored as text
Apply number formats: tenge currency, percent, decimals, thousands separator and date formats
Format cells with fonts, fill, borders, alignment, wrap text and merge & center
Use AutoFill for series and Flash Fill / Smart Fill for patterns
Copy and clear formatting with Format Painter / Paint format and Clear Formats
lessons.theory:
A table full of raw numbers is hard to read. Is `0.15` a price or a discount? Is `45905` a number of products or a date? Good formatting answers these questions at a glance. In this lesson you will learn the three main types of data and how to make a table look clear and professional — a skill every employer expects.

## Three main data types

Every cell contains one of these types:

| Type | Examples | Default alignment | Can you calculate with it? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Number | `250`, `-3.5`, `12000` | Right | Yes |
| Text | `Almaty`, `Order 15`, `ID-007` | Left | No |
| Date / time | `14.03.2025`, `09:30` | Right | Yes (dates are numbers inside) |

> **Tip:** Look at the alignment. If a number is on the **left** side of the cell, the program probably sees it as **text**. Excel also shows a small green triangle in the corner of a "number stored as text".

### Numbers stored as text

Sometimes numbers come from a website or another program as text. They look like numbers, but the program does not count them. For example, `12 000` typed with a space is text in Excel (English settings). The value `'1500` with an apostrophe at the start is also text.

To fix a number stored as text in Excel, select the cell, click the yellow warning sign and choose **Convert to Number**. In both programs you can simply type the number again without spaces.

### Dates are numbers

A date is stored as a **serial number**: the number of days since 30 December 1899. For example, 1 January 2025 is stored as `45658`. The cell only **looks** like a date because of its format. This is why you can subtract dates to count days between them.

> **Remember:** Formatting changes how a value **looks**, not what it **is**. The formula bar shows the real value.

## Quick look: the status bar

Select a range of cells and look at the bottom-right corner of the window. Excel shows **Average**, **Count** and **Sum** of the selected cells in the **status bar**. Google Sheets shows **Sum** in the bottom-right corner; click it to see Average, Count, Min and Max. The Sum includes only real numbers, so it is a quick way to find numbers stored as text.

## Number formats

**Excel:** Home tab > **Number** group. Use the drop-down list, the buttons (Currency, %, comma style, increase/decrease decimals) or **Ctrl+1** for the full **Format Cells** window.
**Google Sheets:** **Format > Number**, or the toolbar buttons (₸/$, %, .0, .00, 123).

| Format | Stored value | Displayed as |
|---|---|---|
| General / Automatic | `1234.5` | `1234.5` |
| Number, 2 decimals, thousands separator | `1234.5` | `1,234.50` |
| Number, 0 decimals | `1234.5` | `1,235` |
| Currency (tenge) | `1234.5` | `1,234.50 ₸` or `₸1,234.50` |
| Percent, 0 decimals | `0.15` | `15%` |
| Percent, 1 decimal | `0.256` | `25.6%` |
| Date `dd.mm.yyyy` | `45730` | `14.03.2025` |
| Date `d mmmm yyyy` | `45730` | `14 March 2025` |

**Worked example 1 – rounding only on screen.** Cell `B2` contains `389990.75`. You choose Number with 0 decimals. The cell shows `389,991`, but the formula bar still shows `389990.75`. If you multiply B2 by 2, the result is `779981.5`, not `779982`.

**Worked example 2 – percent.** Cell `C2` contains `0.15`. With Percent format it shows `15%`. If you type `15` and then apply Percent format, it shows `1500%` — because 15 = 1500%. Type `15%` directly, or type `0.15` first.

### Tenge currency

- **Excel:** Ctrl+1 > **Currency** > in **Symbol** choose `₸ Kazakh (Kazakhstan)`.
- **Google Sheets:** **Format > Number > Custom currency**, search for `tenge` and choose `₸`.

### Custom date formats

- **Excel:** Ctrl+1 > **Custom** > type for example `dd.mm.yyyy`.
- **Google Sheets:** **Format > Number > Custom date and time**, choose the parts you need.

## Fonts, fill, borders and alignment

| Task | Excel (Home tab) | Google Sheets (toolbar / Format menu) |
|---|---|---|
| Bold / italic | **B** / *I* buttons, Ctrl+B / Ctrl+I | **B** / *I* buttons, Ctrl+B / Ctrl+I |
| Font and size | Font box | Font box |
| Fill (background) colour | Paint bucket | Paint bucket ("Fill color") |
| Borders | Borders button | Borders button |
| Horizontal alignment | Align Left / Center / Right | Align button |
| Wrap text | **Wrap Text** | **Text wrapping > Wrap** |
| Merge cells | **Merge & Center** | **Merge cells** |
| Clear formatting | **Clear > Clear Formats** | **Format > Clear formatting** (Ctrl+\\) |

### Wrap text

Long text normally flows into the next cell, or is cut off. **Wrap text** shows it on several lines inside one cell, and the row becomes taller.

### Merge & Center

Merge joins several cells into one big cell. It is useful for a title above a table: select `A1:F1` and click **Merge & Center**. The merged cell has the address of the **top-left** cell (`A1`).

> **Warning:** If several cells have data, merging keeps **only the top-left value**. The other values are deleted. Do not merge cells inside a data table; it makes sorting and filtering difficult.

### Column width and row height

- Drag the border between two column letters to change the width.
- **Double-click** the border to **AutoFit**: the column becomes as wide as its longest value.
- Excel: Home > Format > Column Width. Google Sheets: right-click the column letter > **Resize column**.

If a column is too narrow for a number or date, you see `####`. The value is fine — just make the column wider.

## AutoFill

The small square in the bottom-right corner of the selected cell is the **fill handle**. Drag it down or right to continue a pattern.

| You type | You drag down | You get |
|---|---|---|
| `Monday` | 4 cells | Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday |
| `January` | 3 cells | February, March, April |
| `Lesson 1` | 3 cells | Lesson 2, Lesson 3, Lesson 4 |
| `5` and `10` (select both) | 3 cells | 15, 20, 25 |
| `5` alone | 3 cells | 5, 5, 5 (copies; in Excel hold **Ctrl** to make a series) |

The program sees the **step** between the selected cells and continues it. Double-clicking the fill handle fills down to the end of the neighbour column.

> **Tip:** After the list ends (December, Sunday), AutoFill starts again from the beginning (January, Monday).

## Flash Fill and Smart Fill

These tools find a pattern from **your example** and fill the rest of the column.

Example: column A has full names like `Aidana Seitkali`. You want first names in column B.

1. Type `Aidana` in `B2` (the example).
2. **Excel:** start typing the next one in B3, or press **Ctrl+E** (Data > Flash Fill).
3. **Google Sheets:** start typing in B3. A grey **Smart Fill** suggestion appears; press **Ctrl+Enter** or click the check mark to accept.

Flash Fill writes plain values. If the names in column A change later, column B does not update.

## Format Painter / Paint format

Copy the formatting (not the values) from one cell to others:

1. Click a cell that has the format you like.
2. Excel: click **Format Painter** (paint brush, Home tab). Google Sheets: click **Paint format** (paint roller on the toolbar).
3. Click or drag over the target cells.

Double-click the Format Painter button in Excel to use it many times; press **Esc** to stop.

## Excel vs Google Sheets: quick differences

| Feature | Excel | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|
| Open all format options | Ctrl+1 (Format Cells) | Format > Number > Custom … |
| Pattern fill from example | Flash Fill, Ctrl+E | Smart Fill suggestion, Ctrl+Enter |
| Copy formatting | Format Painter | Paint format |
| Clear formatting | Home > Clear > Clear Formats | Format > Clear formatting, Ctrl+\\ |

On a Mac, use **Cmd** in place of Ctrl (for example Cmd+1 in Excel).

## Summary

- Numbers align right, text aligns left by default; numbers stored as text are not counted.
- Dates are serial numbers formatted to look like dates.
- Number formats change only the display; the formula bar shows the real value.
- Use Percent, Currency (₸) and decimal buttons to make numbers clear.
- Wrap text, merge (only for titles), borders and fill make a table readable.
- `####` means the column is too narrow.
- AutoFill continues series; Flash Fill / Smart Fill copy a pattern from your example.
- Format Painter copies formatting; Clear Formats removes it.

## Key terms

- **Data type** — the kind of value in a cell: number, text, or date/time.
- **Number format** — the way a number is displayed (currency, percent, decimals …).
- **Serial number (date)** — the number of days since 30.12.1899 that stores a date.
- **Status bar** — the bar at the bottom of the window that shows Sum, Count, Average of selected cells.
- **Wrap text** — showing long text on several lines inside one cell.
- **Merge** — joining several cells into one cell.
- **Fill handle** — the small square at the corner of a selection, used for AutoFill.
- **AutoFill** — continuing a series (days, months, numbers) by dragging the fill handle.
- **Flash Fill / Smart Fill** — filling a column from a pattern in your example.
- **Format Painter** — a tool that copies formatting from one cell to others.

practice.title: Find the numbers that are really text
practice.steps:
1. Open `L02-P1_data_types.xlsx`. It is a student's monthly expenses.
2. Look at column B. Which values are on the **left** side of the cell? In Excel, which cells have a small green triangle?
3. Select `B2:B11` and read the **Sum** in the status bar (bottom-right). Text values are not added.
4. Click `C2`. Change its format to **General** (Excel: Home > Number drop-down; Sheets: Format > Number > **Number** or **Automatic**). Read the number. Then press **Ctrl+Z** to undo.
5. In an empty cell, for example `F2`, type `0.256` and apply **Percent** format with **1 decimal**.
6. Answer the questions. (Do not fix the text values before you answer question 1.)
7. Extra: fix the text values (type them again without spaces) and see how the Sum changes.
practice.hint: Numbers are right-aligned and text is left-aligned by default. A number with a space inside, like 12 000, is text.

lessons.title: Formula Basics
lessons.summary: You will be able to write formulas with cell references, control the order of calculation, copy formulas and fix the most common formula errors.
goals: Write formulas that start with = and use the operators + - * / ^
Predict results using the order of operations and parentheses
Use cell references instead of typed numbers so results update automatically
Copy formulas with the fill handle and show formulas with ``Ctrl+` ``
Recognise and fix #DIV/0!, #VALUE!, #NAME?, #REF! and ####
lessons.theory:
Formulas are the real power of a spreadsheet. A formula calculates a result for you, and when the input numbers change, the result changes automatically. A cashier, a teacher or an accountant who uses formulas makes fewer mistakes and saves hours of work every week.

## What is a formula?

A **formula** is an instruction that calculates a value. Every formula **starts with an equals sign** `=`.

| You type | The cell shows | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `5+3` | `5+3` | No `=`, so it is just text |
| `=5+3` | `8` | It is a formula |

After you press **Enter**, the cell shows the **result**. Click the cell again: the **formula bar** shows the formula.

## Arithmetic operators

| Operator | Meaning | Example | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `+` | Addition | `=12+8` | `20` |
| `-` | Subtraction | `=12-8` | `4` |
| `*` | Multiplication | `=12*8` | `96` |
| `/` | Division | `=12/8` | `1.5` |
| `^` | Power (exponent) | `=2^3` | `8` |

> **Remember:** Use `*` for multiplication, not `x` or `×`. Use `/` for division, not `:` or `÷`.

## Order of operations

Spreadsheets follow the same rules as mathematics:

1. **Parentheses** `( )` first
2. **Powers** `^`
3. **Multiplication and division** `*` `/` (from left to right)
4. **Addition and subtraction** `+` `-` (from left to right)

| Formula | Steps | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `=2+3*4` | 3×4 = 12, then 2+12 | `14` |
| `=(2+3)*4` | 2+3 = 5, then 5×4 | `20` |
| `=10-2^2*2` | 2^2 = 4, 4×2 = 8, 10−8 | `2` |
| `=20/4*5` | left to right: 20/4 = 5, 5×5 | `25` |

**Worked example 1 – average of three tests.** A student has 70, 85 and 91 points.

|   | A | B | C | D | E |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Student | Test 1 | Test 2 | Test 3 | Average |
| 2 | Dana Omarova | 70 | 85 | 91 | ? |

- Wrong: `=B2+C2+D2/3` → only D2 is divided: 70 + 85 + 30.33 = **185.33**.
- Correct: `=(B2+C2+D2)/3` → 246 / 3 = **82**.

> **Tip:** When you are not sure about the order, add parentheses. Extra parentheses do not hurt.

## Use cell references, not numbers

You can write `=70+85+91`, but this is a bad habit. If a score changes, the formula does not know. It is much better to use **cell references**: `=B2+C2+D2`.

- When B2 changes, the result changes automatically.
- Other people can see where the numbers come from.

### Three ways to enter a reference

1. **Type** the address: `=B2*C2`.
2. **Click** the cells: type `=`, click B2, type `*`, click C2, press **Enter**.
3. Use the **arrow keys** after `=` to move to the cell you want.

Clicking is faster and prevents typing mistakes.

**Worked example 2 – a shop invoice.**

|   | A | B | C | D |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Item | Qty | Price (₸) | Line total (₸) |
| 2 | Notebook | 5 | 650 | `=B2*C2` → **3250** |
| 3 | Pen | 12 | 180 | `=B3*C3` → **2160** |
| 4 | Backpack | 1 | 14500 | `=B4*C4` → **14500** |
| 5 | | | Subtotal | `=D2+D3+D4` → **19910** |

If the price of a pen changes to 200, D3 becomes 2400 and the subtotal becomes 20150 — automatically.

## Copying formulas with the fill handle

You do not need to type the same formula 100 times.

1. Write the formula in the first row, for example `=B2*C2` in D2.
2. Select D2 and drag the **fill handle** (small square at the bottom-right corner) down.
3. Or **double-click** the fill handle: it fills down as far as the data in the next column goes.

The program **adjusts** the references for each row: D3 gets `=B3*C3`, D4 gets `=B4*C4`, and so on. These are called **relative references**. You will study them in detail in Lesson 4.

Other ways to copy: **Ctrl+C** and **Ctrl+V**, or select D2:D20 and press **Ctrl+D** (fill down).

## Showing formulas

To check your work, you can show all formulas instead of results:

- **Excel:** ``Ctrl+` `` (the key above Tab), or Formulas tab > **Show Formulas**.
- **Google Sheets:** ``Ctrl+` ``, or **View > Show > Formulas**.

Press the same shortcut again to go back to results. On a Mac, use **Cmd+`** in Google Sheets and ``Ctrl+` `` in Excel.

## Common errors and how to fix them

| Error | Meaning | Typical cause | How to fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `#DIV/0!` | Division by zero | The divisor is 0 or an empty cell | Enter the correct divisor, or check the reference |
| `#VALUE!` | Wrong type of value | A formula does math with text, for example `=A2*B2` when B2 is `n/a` | Replace the text with a number |
| `#NAME?` | Unknown name | A typing mistake in a function name, for example `=SUMM(A1:A5)` | Correct the spelling (`SUM`) |
| `#REF!` | Invalid reference | The formula used a cell, row or sheet that was deleted | Rewrite the formula with the correct cell |
| `####` | Not an error in the formula | The column is too narrow for the number or date | Make the column wider |

Excel shows a small green triangle and a warning sign next to many errors. Click the sign to see the explanation. Google Sheets shows a red triangle in the corner; point to the cell to read the message.

> **Warning:** One error spreads. If D5 shows `#VALUE!`, every formula that uses D5 also shows `#VALUE!`. Always fix the **first** error in the chain.

### A fast way to find errors

1. Press ``Ctrl+` `` to show formulas.
2. Look for formulas that are different from their neighbours.
3. Click a cell with an error and read its formula in the formula bar.

## Editing a formula

To change a formula, select the cell and press **F2**, double-click the cell, or click in the formula bar. While you edit, each reference in the formula gets a **colour**, and the same colour frame appears around the cell on the sheet. This helps you see which cells the formula uses. You can even drag a coloured frame to another cell to change the reference.

Press **Enter** to save the change, or **Esc** to cancel it.

**Worked example 3 – a price with delivery.** A customer in Pavlodar buys 3 items at 4 200 ₸ each (B2 = 3, C2 = 4200). Delivery costs 1 500 ₸ (D2 = 1500).

- `=B2*C2+D2` → 12600 + 1500 = **14100** (correct: delivery is paid once).
- `=B2*(C2+D2)` → 3 × 5700 = **17100** (wrong: delivery is paid for each item).

Both formulas have no error message, but only one is correct. The program cannot know what you mean, so always check a result with a quick calculation in your head.

> **Remember:** No error message does not mean the answer is right.

## Excel vs Google Sheets

| Feature | Excel | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|
| Start a formula | `=` | `=` |
| Show formulas | ``Ctrl+` `` or Formulas > Show Formulas | ``Ctrl+` `` or View > Show > Formulas |
| Help while typing | List of functions and argument tips | List of functions and a formula help box |
| Error help | Green triangle + warning button | Red triangle + message on hover |
| Fill down shortcut | Ctrl+D | Ctrl+D |
| Result preview | No | A small grey preview of the result while you type |

## Summary

- A formula always starts with `=`.
- Operators: `+` `-` `*` `/` `^`.
- Order: parentheses, powers, multiply/divide, add/subtract. Use parentheses when you are not sure.
- Use cell references instead of typed numbers so results update automatically.
- Copy a formula with the fill handle; references change for each row.
- ``Ctrl+` `` shows all formulas.
- Learn the errors: `#DIV/0!`, `#VALUE!`, `#NAME?`, `#REF!`, and `####` (column too narrow).

## Key terms

- **Formula** — an instruction that starts with `=` and calculates a value.
- **Operator** — a symbol for a calculation: `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `^`.
- **Order of operations** — the rules that decide which part of a formula is calculated first.
- **Cell reference** — the address of a cell used inside a formula, such as `B2`.
- **Fill handle** — the small square used to copy a formula to nearby cells.
- **Error value** — a special result like `#DIV/0!` that shows something is wrong.
- **Formula bar** — the box that shows the formula of the active cell.

lessons.title: Relative, Absolute and Mixed References
lessons.summary: You will be able to choose the right reference type, lock cells with $ and F4, and use cells from other sheets and named ranges in your formulas.
goals: Predict how relative references change when a formula is copied
Use absolute references ($A$1) for fixed values such as rates and totals
Use mixed references (A$1, $A1) to fill a whole table with one formula
Switch reference types quickly with the F4 key
Reference cells on other sheets and create simple named ranges
lessons.theory:
In Lesson 3 you copied formulas down with the fill handle, and the references changed for each row. This is very useful, but sometimes a reference must **not** change — for example, a tax rate or an exchange rate that sits in one cell. In real work, almost every price list, salary table and report uses this idea. Knowing when to "lock" a reference is one of the most important spreadsheet skills.

## Relative references

A normal reference like `B2` is **relative**. It means "the cell in this position compared to me". When you copy the formula, the reference moves by the same number of rows and columns.

| Formula in D2 | Copied to | Becomes |
|---|---|---|
| `=B2*C2` | D3 (1 row down) | `=B3*C3` |
| `=B2*C2` | D10 (8 rows down) | `=B10*C10` |
| `=B2*C2` | E2 (1 column right) | `=C2*D2` |

Relative references are perfect when each row needs its own data.

## The problem: one fixed cell

**Worked example 1 – exchange rate.** A shop shows prices in tenge and US dollars. The rate is in `F1`.

|   | A | B | C | … | F |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Product | Price (₸) | Price ($) | | 512 |
| 2 | Headphones | 25600 | `=B2/F1` → 50 | | |
| 3 | Mouse | 7680 | ? | | |

You copy C2 down to C3. The formula becomes `=B3/F2`. But F2 is **empty**, so the result is `#DIV/0!`. The reference to the rate moved, and it should not move.

## Absolute references: $A$1

Put a **dollar sign** `$` before the column letter and before the row number: `$F$1`. Now the reference is **absolute** — it never changes when you copy.

- C2: `=B2/$F$1` → 25600 / 512 = **50**
- Copied to C3: `=B3/$F$1` → 7680 / 512 = **15**

`B2` changes to `B3` (relative), but `$F$1` stays `$F$1` (absolute).

> **Remember:** The `$` sign has nothing to do with money. It only means "do not change this part when copying".

## The F4 key

You do not need to type the dollar signs.

1. While typing or editing a formula, put the cursor on a reference (for example `F1`).
2. Press **F4**. Each press changes the type:

| Press F4 | Reference | Type |
|---|---|---|
| 1 time | `$F$1` | Absolute (column and row locked) |
| 2 times | `F$1` | Mixed (row locked) |
| 3 times | `$F1` | Mixed (column locked) |
| 4 times | `F1` | Relative again |

F4 works in Excel and in Google Sheets. On some laptops you must press **Fn+F4**. On a Mac, Excel uses **Cmd+T** (or Fn+F4), and Google Sheets uses **Fn+F4**.

## Mixed references: A$1 and $A1

A **mixed** reference locks only one part:

- `F$1` — the **row** is locked; the column can change. Use it when you copy **across** columns but always need row 1.
- `$A2` — the **column** is locked; the row can change. Use it when you copy **down** rows but always need column A.

| Reference | Copy down 1 row | Copy right 1 column |
|---|---|---|
| `A1` | `A2` | `B1` |
| `$A$1` | `$A$1` | `$A$1` |
| `A$1` | `A$1` | `B$1` |
| `$A1` | `$A2` | `$A1` |

**Worked example 2 – multiplication table.**

|   | A | B | C | D |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | × | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| 2 | 1 | | | |
| 3 | 2 | | | |
| 4 | 3 | | | |

Write in B2: `=$A2*B$1` and copy it to the whole area B2:D4.

- `$A2` always uses column A (the numbers on the left), but the row changes.
- `B$1` always uses row 1 (the numbers on the top), but the column changes.
- D4 gets `=$A4*D$1` → 3 × 3 = **9**. C3 gets `=$A3*C$1` → 2 × 2 = **4**.

One formula fills the whole table. This is the power of mixed references.

## Typical uses

| Task | Formula (first row) | What is locked |
|---|---|---|
| Tax amount | `=B2*$F$1` (F1 = tax rate) | The rate cell |
| Price in dollars | `=B2/$F$1` (F1 = exchange rate) | The rate cell |
| Percentage of total | `=B2/$B$12` (B12 = total) | The total cell |
| Discount grid | `=$A2*(1-B$1)` | Price column and discount row |

**Worked example 3 – percentage of total.**

| City | Sales (₸) | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Almaty | 600000 | `=B2/$B$5` → 50% |
| Astana | 400000 | `=B3/$B$5` → 33.3% |
| Shymkent | 200000 | `=B4/$B$5` → 16.7% |
| **Total** (B5) | 1200000 | 100% |

> **Tip:** Format the share column as **Percent**. The shares together must give 100%. If they do not, check the `$` signs.

## Referencing other sheets

A formula can use a cell on another sheet. Write the sheet name, an exclamation mark `!` and the cell address.

- `=Rates!B1` — cell B1 on the sheet **Rates**.
- `='Sales 2025'!B3` — if the sheet name has a **space** (or starts with a number), put it in **single quotes**.

The easiest way: type `=`, click the other sheet tab, click the cell, press **Enter**. The program writes the correct name and quotes for you.

> **Warning:** If you rename a sheet, formulas update automatically. If you **delete** a sheet, the formulas that use it show `#REF!`.

## Named ranges (basics)

You can give a cell a name, such as `TaxRate`. Then you write `=B2*TaxRate` instead of `=B2*$F$1`. A name works like an absolute reference, and it is easier to read.

**Excel:**

1. Select the cell (for example F1).
2. Click in the **Name Box**, type `TaxRate` and press **Enter**. (Or Formulas > **Define Name**.)

**Google Sheets:**

1. Select the cell.
2. **Data > Named ranges**, type the name, click **Done**.

Rules for names: start with a letter, no spaces (use `Tax_Rate` or `TaxRate`), and do not use a name that looks like a cell address (like `TAX1`).

## Common mistakes

1. **Forgetting the $.** The first row is correct, but all other rows show `#DIV/0!`, `0` or wrong numbers. Check the copied formulas with ``Ctrl+` ``.
2. **Locking too much.** `=$B$2/$B$12` copied down gives the same result in every row, because the sales reference also stopped moving.
3. **Locking the wrong part.** `=B2/B$12` works when you copy down, but `=B2/$B12` does not: the row of the total must be locked, not the column.
4. **Typing the value into the formula.** `=B2*0.12` works, but when the tax rate changes you must edit every formula. Put the rate in one cell and use `$F$1`.

> **Tip:** Before you copy a formula, ask yourself two questions: "When I copy down, which part must stay?" and "When I copy right, which part must stay?"

## Excel vs Google Sheets

| Feature | Excel | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|
| Change reference type | F4 (Mac: Cmd+T) | F4 (Mac: Fn+F4) |
| Reference another sheet | `='Sales 2025'!B3` | `='Sales 2025'!B3` |
| Create a name | Name Box or Formulas > Define Name | Data > Named ranges |
| See all names | Formulas > Name Manager (Ctrl+F3) | Data > Named ranges |

## Summary

- Relative references (`A1`) move when you copy a formula.
- Absolute references (`$A$1`) never move. Use them for one fixed cell: a rate, a total, a setting.
- Mixed references (`A$1`, `$A1`) lock only the row or only the column.
- Press F4 to switch between the four types.
- Use `Sheet!A1` or `'Sheet name'!A1` to get a value from another sheet.
- Named ranges make formulas easier to read and work like absolute references.

## Key terms

- **Relative reference** — a reference that changes when the formula is copied, e.g. `B2`.
- **Absolute reference** — a reference that does not change, e.g. `$B$2`.
- **Mixed reference** — only the row or only the column is locked, e.g. `B$2` or `$B2`.
- **F4** — the key that switches between reference types.
- **Sheet reference** — a reference to a cell on another sheet, e.g. `Rates!B1`.
- **Named range** — a name given to a cell or range, e.g. `TaxRate`.

lessons.title: Essential Functions: SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX, COUNT
lessons.summary: You will be able to summarise any list of numbers with SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX, the COUNT functions and ROUND, quickly and without mistakes.
goals: Write functions with the correct syntax: name, parentheses and arguments
Calculate totals, averages, minimums and maximums with SUM, AVERAGE, MIN and MAX
Count numbers, non-empty cells and empty cells with COUNT, COUNTA and COUNTBLANK
Round values with ROUND, ROUNDUP and ROUNDDOWN, including to tens and hundreds
Use AutoSum, the status bar and the Insert Function menu to work faster
lessons.theory:
Imagine you must add 300 numbers with `=B2+B3+B4+...`. It takes a long time, and it is easy to forget a cell. **Functions** solve this problem. A function is a ready-made formula with a name, like `SUM` or `AVERAGE`. Accountants, sales managers and teachers use these few functions every single day, so they are the best place to start.

## Function syntax

```
=FUNCTION_NAME(argument1, argument2, ...)
```

- It starts with `=`.
- Then the **function name** (capital or small letters both work).
- Then **parentheses** `( )` with the **arguments** — the values the function works with.
- Arguments are separated by **commas** `,`. (On computers with Russian or Kazakh regional settings, Excel and Sheets may use a semicolon `;` instead.)

An argument can be a number (`5`), a cell (`B2`), a range (`B2:B20`) or another formula.

> **Tip:** When you type `=SU`, a list of functions appears. Press **Tab** to choose the selected one. A small help box then shows which arguments the function needs.

## The main functions

| Function | What it does | Example | Result for 10, 20, 30 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SUM` | Adds numbers | `=SUM(B2:B4)` | 60 |
| `AVERAGE` | Arithmetic mean | `=AVERAGE(B2:B4)` | 20 |
| `MIN` | Smallest number | `=MIN(B2:B4)` | 10 |
| `MAX` | Largest number | `=MAX(B2:B4)` | 30 |
| `COUNT` | Counts cells with **numbers** | `=COUNT(B2:B4)` | 3 |
| `COUNTA` | Counts **non-empty** cells (numbers, text, anything) | `=COUNTA(A1:A4)` | — |
| `COUNTBLANK` | Counts **empty** cells | `=COUNTBLANK(B2:B10)` | — |

### Empty cells and text

`SUM`, `AVERAGE`, `MIN`, `MAX` and `COUNT` **ignore** empty cells and text in a range. This matters for `AVERAGE`:

**Worked example 1 – average with a missing score.**

|   | A | B |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Student | Score |
| 2 | Aidana | 80 |
| 3 | Timur | *(empty)* |
| 4 | Madina | 90 |
| 5 | Arman | absent |
| 6 | Dana | 70 |

- `=SUM(B2:B6)` → 80 + 90 + 70 = **240**
- `=AVERAGE(B2:B6)` → 240 / 3 = **80** (the empty cell and "absent" are not counted)
- `=COUNT(B2:B6)` → **3** (only numbers)
- `=COUNTA(B2:B6)` → **4** (80, 90, "absent", 70)
- `=COUNTBLANK(B2:B6)` → **1** (B3)

> **Warning:** An empty cell and a cell with `0` are different. `0` is a number: it is counted by COUNT and it makes the AVERAGE smaller. If a student got 0 points, type 0; if the score is unknown, leave the cell empty.

## Functions with several ranges

You can give a function several arguments, separated by commas:

- `=SUM(B2:B4, B11:B13)` — adds two separate ranges (for example Q1 and Q4).
- `=MAX(B2:B13, D2:D13)` — the largest value in two columns.
- `=SUM(B2:B13, 50000)` — a range plus a number.

To select a second range with the mouse, type the comma, then drag over the next range. Or hold **Ctrl** while you select.

## Rounding: ROUND, ROUNDUP, ROUNDDOWN

Number formatting (Lesson 2) only changes how a number **looks**. The ROUND functions change the **value** itself.

```
=ROUND(number, num_digits)
```

`num_digits` says where to round:

| num_digits | Rounds to | `=ROUND(1234.567, …)` |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | hundredths | 1234.57 |
| 1 | tenths | 1234.6 |
| 0 | whole number | 1235 |
| -1 | tens | 1230 |
| -2 | hundreds | 1200 |

- `ROUND` uses the normal school rule: 5 and more goes up.
- `ROUNDUP` always goes **away from zero**: `=ROUNDUP(1201, -2)` → **1300**.
- `ROUNDDOWN` always goes **towards zero** (cuts off): `=ROUNDDOWN(1299, -2)` → **1200**.

**Worked example 2 – prices with tax.**

| Base price (₸) | With 12% tax | `ROUND(…,0)` | `ROUNDUP(…,-1)` | `ROUNDDOWN(…,-2)` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 990 | 5588.8 | 5589 | 5590 | 5500 |
| 2 345 | 2626.4 | 2626 | 2630 | 2600 |
| 7 345 | 8226.4 | 8226 | 8230 | 8200 |

A shop that wants "nice" prices ending in 0 often uses `=ROUNDUP(B2*1.12, -1)`.

## AutoSum

AutoSum writes a SUM formula for you.

1. Click the empty cell **below** a column of numbers (or to the right of a row).
2. **Excel:** press **Alt+=** or click **AutoSum (Σ)** on the Home tab. **Google Sheets:** click **Functions (Σ)** on the toolbar and choose **SUM**.
3. Check the selected range (it is shown with a moving border) and press **Enter**.

The arrow next to the Σ button also gives Average, Count, Max and Min.

> **Tip:** In Excel, select a whole table plus an empty row below and an empty column on the right, then press **Alt+=**. Excel fills all row and column totals at once.

## Quick statistics in the status bar

Sometimes you do not need a formula — you only want to look at a number.

- **Excel:** select a range; the status bar at the bottom shows **Average**, **Count** and **Sum**. Right-click the status bar to add **Min**, **Max** and **Numerical Count**.
- **Google Sheets:** select a range; the bottom-right corner shows **Sum**. Click it to choose Average, Min, Max, Count or Count Numbers.

The status bar result is not saved in the sheet. Use a formula when the result must stay in the table.

## Inserting a function from the menu

If you do not remember a function name:

- **Excel:** click the **fx** button next to the formula bar (or **Shift+F3**). Search for a function, then fill in the arguments in the **Function Arguments** window. You can also use the **Formulas** tab > Function Library.
- **Google Sheets:** **Insert > Function**, then choose a category (for example Math). The help box shows an example.

## Common mistakes

1. **Including the total in the range.** If B14 has `=SUM(B2:B14)`, the formula uses its own cell. This is a **circular reference**; Excel shows a warning and Sheets shows an error. The range must stop at B13.
2. **Using a colon instead of a comma.** `=SUM(B2:B4:B11:B13)` is not the same as `=SUM(B2:B4,B11:B13)`. Check the coloured frames on the sheet.
3. **Missing parentheses.** `=SUM B2:B10` does not work. Every function needs `( )`.
4. **Numbers stored as text.** SUM ignores them, so the total is too small. Compare COUNT and COUNTA to find them.

> **Remember:** After you write a function, check the result with the status bar. If the two numbers are different, look for a mistake.

## Excel vs Google Sheets

| Feature | Excel | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|
| SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX, COUNT, COUNTA, COUNTBLANK, ROUND… | Yes | Yes (same names and arguments) |
| AutoSum | Alt+= or Home > AutoSum Σ | Toolbar Functions Σ > SUM |
| Insert function window | fx button / Shift+F3 | Insert > Function |
| Status bar stats | Average, Count, Sum (more with right-click) | Sum (click to choose others) |
| Argument separator | `,` (or `;` with some regional settings) | `,` (or `;` with some locales) |

On a Mac, the Excel AutoSum shortcut is **Cmd+Shift+T**.

## Summary

- A function has a name and arguments in parentheses: `=SUM(B2:B10)`.
- SUM, AVERAGE, MIN and MAX ignore empty cells and text.
- COUNT counts numbers, COUNTA counts non-empty cells, COUNTBLANK counts empty cells.
- Use commas to give several ranges: `=SUM(B2:B4, B11:B13)`.
- ROUND changes the value; ROUNDUP always goes up, ROUNDDOWN always goes down; negative digits round to tens, hundreds…
- AutoSum (Alt+= in Excel, Σ in Sheets) builds a SUM quickly; the status bar gives quick answers without formulas.

## Key terms

- **Function** — a ready-made formula with a name, such as `SUM`.
- **Argument** — a value or range given to a function inside the parentheses.
- **Syntax** — the correct way to write a function: name, parentheses, arguments.
- **AutoSum** — a button and shortcut that inserts a SUM formula automatically.
- **COUNT / COUNTA / COUNTBLANK** — count numeric / non-empty / empty cells.
- **ROUND** — rounds a number to a given number of digits.
- **Status bar** — the bar at the bottom that shows quick statistics of a selection.

lessons.title: Text Functions: Split, Clean and Join Text
lessons.summary: You will be able to split, clean, change and join text with formulas, for example to build emails from names or fix messy product codes.
goals: Extract parts of text with LEFT, RIGHT, MID, LEN and FIND or SEARCH
Clean text with TRIM, UPPER, LOWER, PROPER and SUBSTITUTE

Explain the differences between text functions in Excel and Google Sheets
lessons.theory:
Real data is full of text: names, emails, product codes, addresses. Very often the text is not in the form you need. A list has full names but you need first names only, or product codes have extra spaces and mixed letters. Text functions fix these problems in seconds, for thousands of rows, without typing anything again by hand.

## What is a text function?

A **text function** is a function that takes text (also called a **string**) and returns new text or a number about the text. Each character counts: letters, digits, spaces and symbols like `-` or `@`. The first character of a text has **position 1**.

For example, in `Aidana Seitkali` the letter `A` is at position 1, the space is at position 7, and the text has 15 characters.

> **Remember:** text in a formula is always written inside double quotes: `"@college.kz"`, `" "`, `"-"`. Numbers and cell addresses have no quotes.

## Taking parts of text: LEFT, RIGHT, MID

| Function | What it does | Example | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `LEFT(text, n)` | first *n* characters | `=LEFT("Almaty",3)` | `Alm` |
| `RIGHT(text, n)` | last *n* characters | `=RIGHT("EL-1023-KZ",2)` | `KZ` |
| `MID(text, start, n)` | *n* characters from position *start* | `=MID("EL-1023-KZ",4,4)` | `1023` |
| `LEN(text)` | number of characters | `=LEN("Astana")` | `6` |

If you leave out *n* in `LEFT` or `RIGHT`, you get 1 character. `MID` always needs all three arguments.

> **Warning:** `LEFT`, `RIGHT` and `MID` always return **text**, even when the result looks like a number. `MID("EL-1023-KZ",4,4)` gives the text `"1023"`. To turn it into a real number, wrap it in `VALUE`: `=VALUE(MID(A2,4,4))` returns `1023`.

## Finding a position: FIND vs SEARCH

`FIND(find_text, within_text)` and `SEARCH(find_text, within_text)` both return the **position** where some text starts.

| | FIND | SEARCH |
|---|---|---|
| Upper/lower case | case-sensitive (`"a"` is not `"A"`) | not case-sensitive |
| Wildcards `*` and `?` | no | yes |
| Not found | `#VALUE!` error | `#VALUE!` error |

Examples with `A2 = "Kamila Ibraimova"`:

- `=FIND(" ",A2)` returns `7` (the space is the 7th character).
- `=FIND("i",A2)` returns `4` (lower-case *i* in Kamila).
- `=FIND("I",A2)` returns `8` (upper-case *I* in Ibraimova).
- `=SEARCH("I",A2)` returns `4`, because `SEARCH` ignores case.

### Worked example 1: split a full name

| | A | B (first name) | C (last name) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Full name | First name | Last name |
| 2 | Aidana Seitkali | Aidana | Seitkali |

The first name is everything **before** the space. The space is at position `FIND(" ",A2)`, so the first name has one character less:

```
B2: =LEFT(A2, FIND(" ",A2)-1)
```

The last name is everything **after** the space. Total length minus the position of the space gives its length:

```
C2: =RIGHT(A2, LEN(A2)-FIND(" ",A2))
```

Another correct way: `=MID(A2, FIND(" ",A2)+1, 100)`. `MID` simply stops at the end of the text if 100 is more than needed. For `Aidana Seitkali`: `FIND` returns 7, so `LEFT(A2,6)` = `Aidana` and `RIGHT(A2,15-7)` = `RIGHT(A2,8)` = `Seitkali`.

## Cleaning text: TRIM, UPPER, LOWER, PROPER

- `TRIM(text)` removes spaces at the start and the end, and changes double spaces between words into one space. `=TRIM("  Almaty  ")` returns `Almaty`.
- `UPPER(text)` makes all letters capital: `=UPPER("el-1023-kz")` → `EL-1023-KZ`.
- `LOWER(text)` makes all letters small: `=LOWER("ABENOV")` → `abenov`.
- `PROPER(text)` makes the first letter of each word capital: `=PROPER("aidana SEITKALI")` → `Aidana Seitkali`.

You can put functions inside each other (this is called **nesting**): `=UPPER(TRIM(A2))` first removes the spaces, then makes the letters capital.

> **Tip:** extra spaces are invisible but they break things. `"Almaty "` with a space at the end is **not equal** to `"Almaty"`. If a lookup or a comparison does not work, try `TRIM` first. Use `=LEN(A2)` to see hidden spaces: `LEN("Almaty ")` is 7, not 6.

## Replacing text: SUBSTITUTE

`SUBSTITUTE(text, old_text, new_text, [instance])` replaces old text with new text.

- `=SUBSTITUTE("+7 701 234 56 78"," ","")` → `+77012345678` (all spaces removed).
- `=SUBSTITUTE("EL-1023-KZ","-","/")` → `EL/1023/KZ`.
- `=SUBSTITUTE("EL-1023-KZ","-","",1)` → `EL1023-KZ` (only the 1st dash).

`SUBSTITUTE` is case-sensitive, like `FIND`.

## Joining text: &, CONCAT, CONCATENATE, TEXTJOIN

The `&` operator (ampersand, **Shift+7**) joins pieces of text:

```
=B2&" "&C2          →  Aidana Seitkali
=LOWER(B2)&"."&LOWER(C2)&"@college.kz"   →  aidana.seitkali@college.kz
```

Do not forget the space `" "` between words, otherwise you get `AidanaSeitkali`.

The same result with functions:

- `=CONCATENATE(B2," ",C2)` — the old function, works everywhere.
- `=CONCAT(B2," ",C2)` — the newer function in Excel (it also accepts ranges like `A2:C2`).
- `=TEXTJOIN(", ", TRUE, E2:G2)` — joins a whole range and puts a **delimiter** (separator) between the items. `TRUE` means "skip empty cells".

### Worked example 2: emails and logins

| | A | B | C | E (email) | F (login) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | First name | Last name | Year | Email | Login |
| 2 | Dana | Nurlanova | 2024 | dana.nurlanova@college.kz | dnurlanova24 |
| 3 | TIMUR | ospanov | 2025 | timur.ospanov@college.kz | tospanov25 |

```
E2: =LOWER(A2)&"."&LOWER(B2)&"@college.kz"
F2: =LOWER(LEFT(A2,1)&B2)&RIGHT(C2,2)
```

`RIGHT(C2,2)` takes the last two digits of the year. `LOWER` is used because the data has mixed case (row 3).

### Worked example 3: TEXTJOIN skips blanks

| E | F | G | Formula | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| gift | | express | `=TEXTJOIN(", ",TRUE,E2:G2)` | `gift, express` |
| gift | | express | `=E2&", "&F2&", "&G2` | `gift, , express` |

With `&` you get an ugly double comma; `TEXTJOIN` with `TRUE` handles empty cells for you.

## Numbers and dates as text: TEXT

When you join a number with text, the number loses its format. If `C2` contains `125000`, then `="Total: "&C2` shows `Total: 125000`. The `TEXT(value, format)` function formats the number first:

| Formula | Result |
|---|---|
| `=TEXT(125000,"#,##0")` | `125,000` |
| `=TEXT(0.256,"0.0%")` | `25.6%` |
| `=TEXT(42,"0000")` | `0042` (leading zeros) |
| `=TEXT(A2,"dd.mm.yyyy")` (A2 is a date) | `14.03.2025` |
| `=TEXT(A2,"dddd")` | `Friday` |

`"0000"` means "always show 4 digits", which is perfect for codes: `="ALM-"&TEXT(42,"0000")` returns `ALM-0042`.

> **Warning:** format codes inside `TEXT` depend on the language settings of the computer. On a computer with Russian regional settings, Excel may expect `"ДД.ММ.ГГГГ"` instead of `"dd.mm.yyyy"`. Number codes like `"0000"` work everywhere. If a date format code shows strange results, check the language of your Excel or the locale of your Google Sheet (**File > Settings**).

## Excel vs Google Sheets

| Feature | Excel (Microsoft 365) | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|
| `CONCAT` | many values and ranges | **only 2 values**: `=CONCAT(A2,B2)` |
| `CONCATENATE`, `&`, `TEXTJOIN` | yes | yes |
| Split a column by a separator | **Data > Text to Columns** | **Data > Split text to columns**, or the function `=SPLIT(A2," ")` |
| Fill a pattern automatically | **Flash Fill**: type 2 examples, press **Ctrl+E** | **Smart Fill**: Sheets shows a suggestion, accept it |
| Extra functions | `TEXTBEFORE`, `TEXTAFTER`, `TEXTSPLIT` | `SPLIT`, `REGEXEXTRACT`, `REGEXREPLACE` |
| Argument separator | `,` (English) or `;` (Russian/Kazakh settings) | depends on the sheet locale |

> **Tip:** Flash Fill (**Ctrl+E**, on Mac **Cmd+E**) is fast, but it gives fixed values, not formulas. When the source data changes, Flash Fill results do not update. Formulas do.

## Useful shortcuts

| Action | Excel (Windows) | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|
| Edit the active cell | F2 | F2 or Enter |
| Fill formula down | Ctrl+D | Ctrl+D |
| Copy formula to the whole column | double-click the fill handle | double-click the fill handle |
| Show formulas instead of values | ``Ctrl+` `` | ``Ctrl+` `` |

## A good habit: helper columns

Long nested formulas are hard to read and hard to fix. Build them step by step in **helper columns**: first `TRIM`, then `UPPER`, then `MID`. When everything works, you can hide the helper columns or combine the formulas into one.

## Summary

- Text positions start at 1; every space and symbol counts.
- `LEFT`, `RIGHT`, `MID` cut text; `LEN` counts characters.
- `FIND` is case-sensitive; `SEARCH` is not and allows wildcards.
- `TRIM`, `UPPER`, `LOWER`, `PROPER` clean text; `SUBSTITUTE` replaces parts of it.
- `&`, `CONCATENATE`, `CONCAT` and `TEXTJOIN` join text; in Sheets `CONCAT` takes only 2 values.
- `TEXT` formats numbers and dates inside text; `VALUE` turns number-text back into a number.

## Key terms

- **String** — a piece of text in a cell or a formula.
- **Position** — the number of a character in a string, starting from 1.
- **Delimiter** — a character that separates items, for example a comma or a space.
- **Nesting** — putting one function inside another, like `=UPPER(TRIM(A2))`.
- **Case-sensitive** — treats capital and small letters as different.
- **Helper column** — an extra column for a step of a calculation.
- **Format code** — a pattern like `"0000"` or `"#,##0"` that tells `TEXT` how to show a value.

lessons.summary: You will be able to write formulas that make decisions, such as pass/fail, grades, bonuses and discounts, with IF, IFS, AND, OR and NOT.

lessons.theory:
Every day we make decisions with rules: "if the score is 50 or more, the student passes", "if the client is VIP, give 15% discount". A spreadsheet can make these decisions for you, row by row, with **logical functions**. This lesson shows how to write such rules so the sheet decides automatically and never forgets a rule.

## Logical values and comparison operators

A **logical value** (also called a **Boolean** value) is either `TRUE` or `FALSE`. You get a logical value when you compare two things with a **comparison operator**:

| Operator | Meaning | Example (B2 = 72) | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `=` | equal to | `=B2=72` | TRUE |
| `<>` | not equal to | `=B2<>72` | FALSE |
| `>` | greater than | `=B2>80` | FALSE |
| `<` | less than | `=B2<80` | TRUE |
| `>=` | greater than or equal to | `=B2>=72` | TRUE |
| `<=` | less than or equal to | `=B2<=50` | FALSE |

The first `=` starts the formula; the second `=` compares. So `=B2=72` means "is B2 equal to 72?".

You can compare text too: `=C2="Almaty"`. Text must be in double quotes. The comparison is **not case-sensitive**: `"almaty"="ALMATY"` is TRUE in both Excel and Google Sheets.

> **Warning:** `>=` and `<=` are written as two characters, with no space, and the `=` is always second. `=>` is wrong.

## The IF function

`IF` returns one value when a condition is TRUE and another value when it is FALSE:

```
=IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false)
```

### Worked example 1: pass or fail

| | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Student | Score | Result |
| 2 | Aidana Seitkali | 64 | Pass |
| 3 | Timur Ospanov | 50 | Pass |
| 4 | Dana Bekova | 47 | Fail |

```
C2: =IF(B2>=50, "Pass", "Fail")
```

Timur has exactly 50. Because we used `>=`, 50 is a pass. With `>` he would fail. Always think about the **border value**.

### What IF can return

- **Text:** `=IF(B2>=50,"Pass","Fail")` — text in quotes.
- **A number:** `=IF(B2>=50, 1, 0)` — numbers without quotes.
- **A calculation:** `=IF(C2>=D2, C2*5%, 0)` — 5% bonus if sales reach the target.
- **A blank cell:** `=IF(B2<50, "Retake", "")` — two quotes with nothing between them show an empty-looking cell.

> **Tip:** use `""` (empty text) when you want nothing to appear. Do not type a space `" "`: it looks empty but it is not.

## Nested IF: more than two results

Sometimes there are more than two answers, for example grades A, B, C, D, F. You can put an `IF` inside another `IF`. This is a **nested IF**.

| Score | Grade |
|---|---|
| 90 or more | A |
| 75 – 89 | B |
| 60 – 74 | C |
| 50 – 59 | D |
| below 50 | F |

```
=IF(C2>=90,"A",IF(C2>=75,"B",IF(C2>=60,"C",IF(C2>=50,"D","F"))))
```

The sheet checks the conditions **from left to right** and stops at the first TRUE. A score of 82 is not >= 90, but it is >= 75, so the result is `B`. Because it already stopped, it never checks `>=60`.

> **Warning:** the order matters. If you start with `IF(C2>=50,"D", …)`, every score of 50 or more becomes `D`, even 98. When you use `>=`, start from the **largest** border. Also count the brackets: 4 IFs need 4 closing brackets at the end.

## IFS: many conditions without nesting

`IFS` (Excel 2019, Microsoft 365 and Google Sheets) takes pairs of *condition, value*:

```
=IFS(C2>=90,"A", C2>=75,"B", C2>=60,"C", C2>=50,"D", TRUE,"F")
```

The last pair `TRUE,"F"` means "in all other cases". Without it, a score below 50 returns the `#N/A` error, because no condition is TRUE.

## AND, OR, NOT

| Function | Returns TRUE when… | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `AND(c1, c2, …)` | **all** conditions are TRUE | `=AND(C2>=D2, E2<=2)` |
| `OR(c1, c2, …)` | **at least one** condition is TRUE | `=OR(F2>=4.8, C2>=3000000)` |
| `NOT(c)` | the condition is FALSE | `=NOT(G2="Yes")` |

Alone, these functions return only TRUE or FALSE. They become powerful **inside IF**.

### Worked example 2: bonus with AND

A manager gets a 5% bonus only if sales reach the target **and** they were absent 2 days or fewer.

| | A | B (Sales) | C (Target) | D (Days absent) | E (Bonus) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | Arman | 2,300,000 | 2,000,000 | 1 | 115,000 |
| 3 | Saule | 2,600,000 | 2,500,000 | 4 | 0 |
| 4 | Miras | 1,700,000 | 2,000,000 | 0 | 0 |

```
E2: =IF(AND(B2>=C2, D2<=2), B2*5%, 0)
```

Saule reached the target but was absent 4 days, so `AND` is FALSE. Miras had no absences but did not reach the target.

### Worked example 3: discount with OR and nested IF

A shop gives free delivery if the city is Almaty **or** the order is 30,000 ₸ or more; otherwise delivery costs 1,500 ₸:

```
=IF(OR(C2="Almaty", D2>=30000), 0, 1500)
```

Discount rules, checked in this order: VIP clients get 15%; students with an order of 20,000 ₸ or more get 10%; any other order of 50,000 ₸ or more gets 5%; everybody else gets 0%.

```
=IF(B2="VIP",15%,IF(AND(B2="Student",D2>=20000),10%,IF(D2>=50000,5%,0)))
```

| Type | Amount | Discount | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| VIP | 12,000 | 15% | first rule |
| Student | 25,000 | 10% | second rule |
| Student | 15,000 | 0% | too small for rule 2 and rule 3 |
| Regular | 64,000 | 5% | third rule |

### Handling empty cells

If the amount is not entered yet, the formula should show nothing:

```
=IF(D2="", "", D2*(1-F2))
```

`D2=""` is TRUE when D2 is empty. `SUM` ignores the `""` results, so totals still work.

## Excel vs Google Sheets

| Topic | Excel (Microsoft 365) | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|
| `IF`, `AND`, `OR`, `NOT` | yes | yes |
| `IFS`, `SWITCH` | Excel 2019 and newer | yes |
| Help while typing | tooltip with argument names | yellow help box; press **F1** to show/hide it |
| Argument separator | `,` or `;` (depends on regional settings) | `,` or `;` (depends on sheet locale) |
| Text comparison | not case-sensitive | not case-sensitive |
| `TRUE`/`FALSE` shown as | `TRUE`/`FALSE` | `TRUE`/`FALSE` (can be shown as checkboxes) |

> **Tip:** in Google Sheets you can turn TRUE/FALSE cells into checkboxes: **Insert > Checkbox**. A ticked box is TRUE. In Microsoft 365 Excel there is also **Insert > Checkbox** in new versions.

## Common errors

- `#NAME?` — usually text without quotes: `=IF(B2>=50,Pass,Fail)` is wrong.
- Wrong result for numbers — a number in quotes is text: `"50"` is not the number 50. Write `B2>=50`.
- `#N/A` from `IFS` — no condition was TRUE; add `TRUE,"…"` at the end.
- Missing or extra brackets — the cell shows an error message. Both programs colour each pair of brackets so you can count them.

## Useful shortcuts

| Action | Excel (Windows) | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|
| Fill formula down | Ctrl+D | Ctrl+D |
| Make a reference absolute (`$`) | F4 | F4 |
| Insert a function | Shift+F3 | type `=` and the name |
| Undo | Ctrl+Z (Mac: Cmd+Z) | Ctrl+Z |

## Summary

- Comparison operators `=`, `<>`, `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=` return TRUE or FALSE.
- `IF(test, if_true, if_false)` returns text, numbers, calculations or `""`.
- In a nested `IF` or `IFS`, conditions are checked in order; start from the largest border.
- `AND` needs all conditions TRUE; `OR` needs at least one; `NOT` reverses a condition.
- Put `AND`/`OR`/`NOT` inside `IF` to make real business rules.
- Always test border values like exactly 50 or exactly the target.

## Key terms

- **Logical value (Boolean)** — TRUE or FALSE.
- **Comparison operator** — a sign that compares two values, such as `>=`.
- **Condition (logical test)** — an expression that is TRUE or FALSE.
- **Nested IF** — an IF function inside another IF.
- **Border value** — the value exactly on the limit of a rule, like 50 for "50 or more".
- **Empty text** — `""`, a result that shows an empty-looking cell.

lessons.theory:
`SUM`, `COUNT` and `AVERAGE` work with **all** numbers in a range. But a manager usually asks questions with a condition: "How much did we sell **in Almaty**?", "How many orders were **over 500,000 ₸**?", "What was the average laptop sale **in March**?". Conditional aggregation functions answer these questions with one formula, and the answer updates when new data is added.

## What is a criterion?

A **criterion** (plural: **criteria**) is the condition that decides which rows are included. A **criteria range** is the column that is checked. To **aggregate** means to combine many values into one number: a count, a sum, an average, a maximum or a minimum.

## One condition: COUNTIF, SUMIF, AVERAGEIF

```
=COUNTIF(criteria_range, criterion)
=SUMIF(criteria_range, criterion, [sum_range])
=AVERAGEIF(criteria_range, criterion, [average_range])
```

### Worked example 1

| | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | City | Category | Amount |
| 2 | Almaty | Phones | 89,990 |
| 3 | Astana | Laptops | 249,990 |
| 4 | Almaty | Laptops | 219,990 |
| 5 | Shymkent | Phones | 399,990 |
| 6 | Almaty | Accessories | 9,990 |

| Question | Formula | Result |
|---|---|---|
| How many orders from Almaty? | `=COUNTIF(A2:A6,"Almaty")` | 3 |
| Total amount for Almaty | `=SUMIF(A2:A6,"Almaty",C2:C6)` | 319,970 |
| Average amount for Phones | `=AVERAGEIF(B2:B6,"Phones",C2:C6)` | 244,990 |

`SUMIF` checks column A, but adds the numbers from column C **in the same rows**.

> **Remember:** the criteria range and the sum range must have the **same size** and start in the same row: `A2:A6` with `C2:C6`, not `C3:C7`.

Text criteria are **not case-sensitive**: `"almaty"` and `"ALMATY"` give the same result.

## Criteria with numbers and operators

To compare numbers, write the operator and the number **together inside quotes**:

| Criterion | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `500000` or `"500000"` | equal to 500,000 | `=COUNTIF(C2:C151,500000)` |
| `">=500000"` | 500,000 or more | `=COUNTIF(C2:C151,">=500000")` |
| `"<50000"` | less than 50,000 | `=SUMIF(C2:C151,"<50000")` |
| `"<>Almaty"` | not Almaty | `=COUNTIF(A2:A151,"<>Almaty")` |
| `""` | empty cells | `=COUNTIF(D2:D151,"")` |

If you leave out `sum_range`, `SUMIF` adds the cells of the criteria range itself. So `=SUMIF(H2:H151,">10")` adds all units bigger than 10.

## Criteria from a cell

Typing the limit inside the formula is not flexible. Put the limit in a cell, for example `M1 = 200000`, and join it to the operator with `&`:

```
=COUNTIF(J2:J151, ">="&M1)
```

Now you only change `M1`, and the result updates. Without the operator, just use the cell: `=SUMIF(C2:C151, P2, J2:J151)` sums the amount for the city written in `P2`.

> **Warning:** `">=M1"` in quotes does not work: the program looks for the text "M1". The operator goes in quotes, the cell address stays **outside**: `">="&M1`.

## Many conditions: COUNTIFS, SUMIFS, AVERAGEIFS, MAXIFS, MINIFS

These functions accept **pairs** of *criteria_range, criterion*. A row is included only when **all** conditions are TRUE (like `AND`).

```
=COUNTIFS(range1, crit1, range2, crit2, …)
=SUMIFS(sum_range, range1, crit1, range2, crit2, …)
=AVERAGEIFS(average_range, range1, crit1, …)
=MAXIFS(max_range, range1, crit1, …)
=MINIFS(min_range, range1, crit1, …)
```

> **Warning:** the argument order is different! In `SUMIF` the sum range is **last**. In `SUMIFS`, `AVERAGEIFS`, `MAXIFS` and `MINIFS` the range to calculate is **first**.

### Worked example 2

Using the table from example 1:

| Question | Formula | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Almaty laptops: total | `=SUMIFS(C2:C6,A2:A6,"Almaty",B2:B6,"Laptops")` | 219,990 |
| Phone orders of 100,000 ₸ or more | `=COUNTIFS(B2:B6,"Phones",C2:C6,">=100000")` | 1 |
| Biggest Almaty order | `=MAXIFS(C2:C6,A2:A6,"Almaty")` | 219,990 |
| Smallest Almaty order | `=MINIFS(C2:C6,A2:A6,"Almaty")` | 9,990 |

`COUNTIFS` can also use one column twice. This is how you count a **range of values or dates**, for example all orders in March 2025:

```
=SUMIFS(J2:J151, B2:B151, ">="&DATE(2025,3,1), B2:B151, "<="&DATE(2025,3,31))
```

## Wildcards: * and ?

In text criteria you can use **wildcards**:

- `*` — any number of characters (also zero).
- `?` — exactly one character.

| Criterion | Matches | Does not match |
|---|---|---|
| `"Samsung*"` | Samsung Galaxy A15, Samsung TV 43 | JBL Headphones |
| `"*TV*"` | Samsung TV 43, LG TV 50 | iPhone 15 |
| `"PH-???"` | PH-101, PH-305 | PH-2040, PH-4410 |
| `"*case"` | Phone case | Phone cases |

To find a real star or question mark, put a tilde before it: `"~*"`.

## Building a summary table

A **summary table** shows one number for every combination of two things, for example City × Category. One formula, copied to all cells, can fill it if you use **mixed references**:

| | A | B | C | D |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | City | Phones | Laptops | Total |
| 2 | Almaty | ? | ? | ? |
| 3 | Astana | ? | ? | ? |

```
B2: =SUMIFS(Sales!$J:$J, Sales!$C:$C, $A2, Sales!$E:$E, B$1)
```

- `Sales!$J:$J` — the amount column on the sheet **Sales**, fully fixed.
- `$A2` — the column is fixed (always the city in column A), the row changes.
- `B$1` — the row is fixed (always the category in row 1), the column changes.

Copy `B2` to the right and down. Then add a **Total** column with `SUM` and check: the grand total of the summary must be the same as `=SUM(Sales!J:J)`. This is a simple and important **control check**.

> **Tip:** press **F4** after typing a reference to cycle through `$A$2`, `A$2`, `$A2`, `A2`. On a Mac use **Cmd+T** in Excel; in Google Sheets **F4** works in both systems (on some laptops **Fn+F4**).

## Excel vs Google Sheets

| Topic | Excel (Microsoft 365) | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|
| `COUNTIF(S)`, `SUMIF(S)`, `AVERAGEIF(S)` | yes | yes |
| `MAXIFS`, `MINIFS` | Excel 2019 and newer | yes |
| Wildcards `*` `?` `~` | yes | yes |
| Whole-column references `J:J` | yes | yes |
| Reference to another sheet | `Sales!J2:J151` (quotes if the name has spaces: `'Sales 2025'!J2`) | same |
| Extra tools | PivotTables (lesson 12) | `QUERY`, pivot tables, `COUNTUNIQUEIFS` |

## Common mistakes

- Ranges of different size in `SUMIF`/`SUMIFS` → wrong result or `#VALUE!`.
- Operator outside the quotes: `=COUNTIF(J2:J151,>=500000)` → error.
- Cell inside the quotes: `">=M1"` → result 0.
- Extra spaces in the data (`"Almaty "`) → those rows are not counted. Clean data with `TRIM` first.
- Numbers stored as text are not summed. They are often aligned to the left.

## Summary

- `COUNTIF`, `SUMIF`, `AVERAGEIF` use one condition; the `…IFS` versions use many (all must be TRUE).
- Operators go inside quotes: `">=50"`, `"<>Almaty"`.
- Join an operator with a cell using `&`: `">="&M1`.
- `*` means any characters, `?` means exactly one character.
- In `SUMIFS`, `AVERAGEIFS`, `MAXIFS`, `MINIFS` the calculation range comes first.
- Build summary tables with one formula and mixed references, then check the grand total.

## Key terms

- **Criterion / criteria** — the condition that selects rows.
- **Criteria range** — the range that is checked against the criterion.
- **Sum range** — the range whose numbers are added.
- **Aggregate** — to combine many values into one result (count, sum, average, max, min).
- **Wildcard** — a symbol that stands for unknown characters (`*`, `?`).
- **Mixed reference** — a reference with only the column or only the row fixed, like `$A2` or `B$1`.
- **Summary table** — a small table of totals for combinations of categories.

lessons.title: Dates and Times: Calculations with Calendars and Clocks
lessons.summary: You will be able to calculate ages, years of service, deadlines, working days and hours worked with date and time functions.
goals: Explain how dates and times are stored as serial numbers and fractions
Enter dates correctly and take them apart with YEAR, MONTH, DAY, WEEKDAY and TEXT
Calculate ages and service with DATEDIF, and future dates with EDATE and EOMONTH
Count working days and find due dates with NETWORKDAYS and WORKDAY
Calculate hours worked, including overnight shifts, and convert time to hours
lessons.theory:
Dates and times are everywhere in work: deadlines, birthdays, hire dates, working hours, delivery days. A spreadsheet can calculate age, years of service, the number of working days in a project, or a salary from hours worked. To do this correctly, you first need to understand how Excel and Google Sheets store dates and times.

## How dates are stored: serial numbers

For the spreadsheet, a **date is a number**. It counts days from a start point. This number is called a **serial number** (or date value):

| Date | Serial number |
|---|---|
| 1 January 1900 | 1 (Excel) |
| 1 January 2025 | 45658 |
| 2 January 2025 | 45659 |
| 1 September 2025 | 45901 |

Because a date is a number, you can do maths with it:

- `=A2+30` — the date 30 days later.
- `=B2-A2` — the number of days between two dates.

You see a normal date only because the cell has a **date format**. Change the format to **Number** and you see the serial number. Change it back to **Date** and the date returns.

**Time** is a part of a day: 12:00 = 0.5, 06:00 = 0.25, 18:00 = 0.75. So `2025-09-01 18:00` is stored as 45901.75.

> **Remember:** if a date shows as a number like `45901`, nothing is broken — only the format is wrong. Choose **Home > Number Format > Short Date** in Excel or **Format > Number > Date** in Sheets.

## Entering dates

How you type a date depends on the **regional settings** (locale). In Kazakhstan computers often use `dd.mm.yyyy`, for example `14.03.2025`. A US setting expects `3/14/2025`. If the date stays on the **left side** of the cell, it was not understood: it is just text.

> **Tip:** the format `2025-03-14` (year-month-day) is understood almost everywhere. Inside formulas, use the `DATE` function, which does not depend on settings: `=DATE(2025,3,14)`.

In Google Sheets the locale is set in **File > Settings > Locale**. In Excel it comes from Windows regional settings.

## Date functions

| Function | Returns | Example (A2 = 14.03.2025) | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `TODAY()` | today's date | `=TODAY()` | changes every day |
| `NOW()` | today's date and the current time | `=NOW()` | changes all the time |
| `DATE(y,m,d)` | a date from 3 numbers | `=DATE(2025,3,14)` | 14.03.2025 |
| `YEAR(date)` | the year | `=YEAR(A2)` | 2025 |
| `MONTH(date)` | the month number | `=MONTH(A2)` | 3 |
| `DAY(date)` | the day of the month | `=DAY(A2)` | 14 |
| `WEEKDAY(date,2)` | day of the week, Monday = 1 … Sunday = 7 | `=WEEKDAY(A2,2)` | 5 (Friday) |
| `TEXT(date,"dddd")` | the day name | `=TEXT(A2,"dddd")` | Friday |
| `TEXT(date,"mmmm")` | the month name | `=TEXT(A2,"mmmm")` | March |

`TODAY` and `NOW` are **volatile**: they recalculate every time the file changes or opens. For reports that must not change, type a fixed **report date** in a cell and use that cell.

`WEEKDAY` without the second argument starts with **Sunday = 1**. With `2` it starts with **Monday = 1**, which is the normal week in Kazakhstan. A weekend test is simply `=WEEKDAY(A2,2)>5`.

`DATE` is also smart with overflow: `=DATE(2025,13,1)` is 1 January 2026. So `=DATE(YEAR(A2),MONTH(A2)+1,1)` is the first day of the next month.

## Differences between dates: DATEDIF

A simple subtraction gives days. For full years or full months use `DATEDIF(start, end, unit)`:

| Unit | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `"y"` | full years |
| `"m"` | full months |
| `"d"` | days |
| `"ym"` | months left after the full years |

### Worked example 1: age and years of service

Report date in `B1`: 01.09.2025.

| Employee | Birth date (B) | Hire date (C) | Age | Years of service | Months of service |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Aidana Seitkali | 14.03.2006 | 10.02.2021 | 19 | 4 | 54 |

```
Age:               =DATEDIF(B4,$B$1,"y")
Years of service:  =DATEDIF(C4,$B$1,"y")
Months of service: =DATEDIF(C4,$B$1,"m")
```

From 10.02.2021 to 01.09.2025 there are 4 full years and 6 full months (54 months), because 1 September comes before 10 September.

> **Warning:** in Excel, `DATEDIF` is a "hidden" function: it works, but Excel does not suggest it while you type and has no help tooltip. Type it carefully. The start date must be **earlier** than the end date, or you get `#NUM!`.

## Adding months: EDATE and EOMONTH

- `EDATE(date, months)` — the same day, *months* later (or earlier with a negative number). A 3-month probation that starts on 10.02.2021 ends on `=EDATE(C4,3)` = 10.05.2021.
- `EOMONTH(date, months)` — the **last day** of the month. `=EOMONTH(C4,0)` = 28.02.2021, `=EOMONTH(C4,1)` = 31.03.2021.

Both functions return a serial number, so format the result cells as **Date**.

## Working days: NETWORKDAYS and WORKDAY

Business counts only **working days** (Monday–Friday, without public holidays).

- `NETWORKDAYS(start, end, [holidays])` — the number of working days between two dates, **including** both dates.
- `WORKDAY(start, days, [holidays])` — the date that is *days* working days after the start.

The holidays are a range of dates, for example `Holidays!$A$2:$A$16`.

### Worked example 2: a project with a holiday

Holiday list contains 10.03.2025 (a day off).

| Formula | Result | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `=DATE(2025,3,14)-DATE(2025,3,3)` | 11 | calendar days |
| `=NETWORKDAYS(DATE(2025,3,3),DATE(2025,3,14),H2:H16)` | 9 | 10 weekdays minus 1 holiday |
| `=WORKDAY(DATE(2025,3,7),5,H2:H16)` | 17.03.2025 | Monday 10 March is skipped |

> **Tip:** if your weekend is not Saturday–Sunday (for example a 6-day work week), use `NETWORKDAYS.INTL` and `WORKDAY.INTL`. They exist in both programs.

## Time calculations

Time is a fraction of a day, so `End - Start` gives a fraction. To get **hours as a number**, multiply by 24.

### Worked example 3: hours worked and pay

| Start | End | Break (min) | Hours | Pay at 2,000 ₸/h |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 09:00 | 18:00 | 60 | 8 | 16,000 |
| 22:00 | 06:30 | 30 | 8 | 16,000 |

```
Hours (day shift):   =(D2-C2)*24 - E2/60
Hours (any shift):   =MOD(D2-C2,1)*24 - E2/60
Pay:                 =G2*F2
```

For a **night shift** the end time is smaller than the start time, so `D2-C2` is negative. Excel shows `#####` for a negative time. `MOD(D2-C2,1)` adds one full day when the result is negative: 06:30 − 22:00 = −15.5 hours → MOD gives 8.5 hours. Minus a 30-minute break: 8 hours.

> **Warning:** if you sum times and keep the time format, a total of 30 hours shows as `06:00`. Use the custom format `[h]:mm`, or multiply by 24 and use a Number format. Multiply by 24 **before** multiplying by a rate in tenge.

## Excel vs Google Sheets

| Topic | Excel (Microsoft 365) | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|
| Insert today's date (fixed) | **Ctrl+;** | **Ctrl+;** |
| Insert current time (fixed) | **Ctrl+Shift+;** | **Ctrl+Shift+;** |
| Date settings | Windows regional settings | **File > Settings > Locale** |
| `DATEDIF` | works, but hidden (no tooltip) | works, with help |
| Date picker | no (only in some add-ins) | double-click a date cell with data validation (date) |
| Format for long total hours | Custom `[h]:mm` | **Format > Number > Duration** |

On a Mac in Excel, use **Cmd+;** for the date.

## Summary

- Dates are serial numbers (days); times are fractions of a day.
- Use `DATE(y,m,d)` in formulas; `YEAR`, `MONTH`, `DAY`, `WEEKDAY(date,2)` take dates apart.
- Subtract dates for days; use `DATEDIF` for full years or months.
- `EDATE` adds months; `EOMONTH` gives the end of a month.
- `NETWORKDAYS` and `WORKDAY` skip weekends and a holiday list.
- Hours = `MOD(end-start,1)*24`; this works for night shifts too.
- For stable reports use a fixed report date instead of `TODAY()`.

## Key terms

- **Serial number** — the number that stores a date (days since the start date).
- **Locale** — regional settings that control how dates and numbers are typed and shown.
- **Volatile function** — a function that recalculates every time, like `TODAY` or `NOW`.
- **Working day** — a weekday that is not a public holiday.
- **Overnight shift** — a shift that ends on the next day.
- **Duration** — a length of time, like 8:30 hours, not a time of day.

lessons.title: Sorting, Filtering and Conditional Formatting
lessons.summary: You will be able to sort and filter a table, total only the visible rows, and colour cells or whole rows automatically with conditional formatting rules.
goals: Sort a table by one or several levels, and by colour
Filter rows by values, text, numbers and dates, and clear filters
