lessons.theory:
A table with 60 or 6,000 rows is hard to read. A manager wants to see the best sellers first, only one city, or every employee with very high sales in green. **Sorting** changes the order of rows, **filtering** hides rows you do not need, and **conditional formatting** colours cells automatically by rules. These three tools turn a long list into information you can see in a few seconds.

## Sorting

**Sorting** puts rows in order: A→Z, Z→A, smallest→largest, oldest→newest. The whole row moves together.

### Single-level sort

1. Click **one cell** in the column you want to sort by (for example, any cell in *Sales*).
2. Excel: **Data > Sort A to Z** (smallest to largest) or **Sort Z to A**. Sheets: **Data > Sort sheet > Sort sheet (A to Z)**, or **Data > Sort range** for a selected range.

> **Warning:** never select only one column and sort it. If Excel asks, choose **Expand the selection**. Otherwise only that column moves and every row gets the wrong data: names no longer match their sales. Press **Ctrl+Z** at once if this happens.

### Multi-level sort

Sometimes one level is not enough: you want cities A→Z, and **inside each city** the biggest sales first.

1. Click a cell inside the table.
2. Excel: **Data > Sort** opens the Sort dialog. Tick **My data has headers**. Choose *Sort by* **City**, *Order* **A to Z**. Click **Add Level**, choose *Then by* **Sales 2025**, *Order* **Largest to Smallest**. Click **OK**.
3. Sheets: select the whole table, **Data > Sort range > Advanced range sorting options**. Tick **Data has header row**, sort by **City A→Z**, click **Add another sort column**, choose **Sales Z→A**, click **Sort**.

### Worked example 1: two-level sort

| Name | City | Sales |
|---|---|---|
| Dana | Astana | 12,000,000 |
| Arman | Almaty | 9,500,000 |
| Saule | Astana | 21,300,000 |
| Miras | Almaty | 18,700,000 |

After sorting by City (A→Z), then Sales (largest→smallest):

| Name | City | Sales |
|---|---|---|
| Miras | Almaty | 18,700,000 |
| Arman | Almaty | 9,500,000 |
| Saule | Astana | 21,300,000 |
| Dana | Astana | 12,000,000 |

### Sort by colour

If some cells have a fill colour (typed by hand or from conditional formatting), you can put the coloured rows on top. Excel: in the Sort dialog choose *Sort On* **Cell Color** and the colour, *On Top*. Sheets: create a filter, open the filter menu of the column, **Sort by color > Fill color**.

## Filtering

A **filter** hides the rows that do not match a condition. The data is not deleted; it is only hidden. Row numbers of the visible rows turn **blue**, and you see gaps in the numbers.

### Turning on a filter

- Excel: click inside the table, **Data > Filter**, or **Ctrl+Shift+L**. Small arrows appear in the header row.
- Sheets: **Data > Create a filter**, or the **Filter** button on the toolbar.

Click the arrow of a column to choose:

| Filter type | Example | Excel | Sheets |
|---|---|---|---|
| By values | only *Astana* | tick boxes in the list | **Filter by values** |
| Text filter | name begins with "A" | **Text Filters > Begins With** | **Filter by condition > Text starts with** |
| Number filter | sales greater than 15,000,000 | **Number Filters > Greater Than** | **Filter by condition > Greater than** |
| Date filter | hired in 2023 | tick 2023 in the date tree, or **Date Filters** | **Filter by condition > Date is after/before**, or tick values |
| Top items | 10 biggest sales | **Number Filters > Top 10** | not available (use sorting) |

Filters in several columns work together like **AND**: City = Almaty **and** Rating ≥ 4.5.

### Clearing filters

- Clear one column: open its arrow, **Clear Filter From…** (Excel) or tick **Select all** (Sheets).
- Clear all: Excel **Data > Clear**. Sheets: **Data > Remove filter** (this also removes the arrows).
- Excel shows "*12 of 60 records found*" in the status bar while a filter is on.

### Filter views (Google Sheets)

When many people edit one Google Sheet, a normal filter changes the view **for everybody**. A **filter view** is a personal, named filter: **Data > Filter views > Create new filter view**. The frame turns dark grey. Other users do not see your filter, and you can save it and open it later. In Microsoft 365 Excel a similar tool is **View > Sheet View > New**.

### SUBTOTAL: totals of visible rows only

`SUM` adds all rows, also hidden ones. `SUBTOTAL` calculates only the **visible** rows of a filtered list:

```
=SUBTOTAL(9, F2:F61)    sum of visible rows
=SUBTOTAL(3, B2:B61)    count of visible non-empty cells
=SUBTOTAL(1, G2:G61)    average of visible rows
```

| Code | Function | Code (also ignores manually hidden rows) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | AVERAGE | 101 |
| 3 | COUNTA | 103 |
| 4 | MAX | 104 |
| 9 | SUM | 109 |

### Worked example 2: SUBTOTAL with a filter

A list of 60 employees, total sales 1,000,000,000 ₸. Filter Department = Online, 18 rows visible with 320,000,000 ₸.

| Formula | Result with filter | Result without filter |
|---|---|---|
| `=SUM(F2:F61)` | 1,000,000,000 | 1,000,000,000 |
| `=SUBTOTAL(9,F2:F61)` | 320,000,000 | 1,000,000,000 |
| `=SUBTOTAL(3,B2:B61)` | 18 | 60 |

> **Tip:** put `SUBTOTAL` formulas **below** the table with one empty row between, or above the header. Then the filter does not hide them. In Excel, **AutoSum (Alt+=)** under a filtered column writes `SUBTOTAL(9,…)` for you.

## Conditional formatting

**Conditional formatting** changes the look of a cell (fill, font colour, bars, icons) when a rule is TRUE. When the data changes, the colours change too.

- Excel: select the range, **Home > Conditional Formatting**.
- Sheets: select the range, **Format > Conditional formatting**. A panel opens on the right.

### Rule types

| Rule | What it does | Excel | Sheets |
|---|---|---|---|
| Highlight cell rules | greater than, less than, between, equal to, text contains, date, duplicates | **Highlight Cells Rules** | **Single color > Format cells if…** |
| Top/Bottom | top 10 items, top 10%, above average | **Top/Bottom Rules** | custom formula, e.g. `=F2>=LARGE($F$2:$F$61,10)` |
| Data bars | a bar inside the cell, longer for bigger values | **Data Bars** | not available (use `SPARKLINE`) |
| Colour scales | colour from red (low) to green (high) | **Color Scales** | **Color scale** tab |
| Icon sets | arrows, traffic lights, stars | **Icon Sets** | not available |
| Custom formula | any rule you write | **New Rule > Use a formula…** | **Custom formula is** |

### Custom formula rules: highlight a whole row

To colour the **whole row** when sales are over 20,000,000 ₸:

1. Select the whole data range **without the header**, for example `A2:G61`.
2. Excel: **Home > Conditional Formatting > New Rule > Use a formula to determine which cells to format**. Sheets: **Format > Conditional formatting > Format cells if… > Custom formula is**.
3. Type the formula for the **first row** of the range:

```
=$F2>20000000
```

4. Choose a fill colour, click **OK** / **Done**.

The `$` before `F` locks the column: every cell in row 2 (A2, B2 … G2) checks `F2`. The row number has no `$`, so row 3 checks `F3`, and so on.

### Worked example 3: which rows are coloured?

| Row | Name | City | Sales | Rating | `=$D2>20000000` | `=AND($C2="Shymkent",$E2>=4.5)` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | Aigerim | Almaty | 24,100,000 | 4.1 | yes | no |
| 3 | Bekzat | Shymkent | 8,300,000 | 4.7 | no | yes |
| 4 | Inkar | Shymkent | 19,900,000 | 4.2 | no | no |

> **Warning:** the most common mistake is `=F2>20000000` without `$`. Then cell B2 checks C2, cell C2 checks D2 … and the colours look random. Another mistake is `=$F$2`: then every row checks only row 2.

### Managing rules

- Excel: **Home > Conditional Formatting > Manage Rules**. Here you can edit, delete, change the **Applies to** range and the order of rules. Rules higher in the list win when two rules set the same format.
- Sheets: the conditional formatting panel lists all rules for the selected range. Drag a rule to change its order. The first matching rule wins.
- To remove all rules: Excel **Clear Rules > Clear Rules from Entire Sheet**; Sheets: delete each rule with the bin icon.

## Excel vs Google Sheets

| Topic | Excel | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|
| Turn filter on/off | Data > Filter, **Ctrl+Shift+L** | Data > Create a filter / Remove filter |
| Personal filter | View > Sheet View (Microsoft 365) | **Filter views** |
| Multi-level sort | Data > Sort > Add Level | Data > Sort range > Advanced options |
| Data bars, icon sets | yes | no |
| Top 10 rule | built-in | custom formula with `LARGE` |
| Shortcuts on Mac | **Cmd+Shift+F** for filter | same menus |

## Summary

- Always sort the whole table; use **Add Level** for multi-level sorts.
- Filters hide rows; several column filters work like AND; clear them when finished.
- In Sheets, filter views let each user filter without changing the view for others.
- `SUBTOTAL(9,…)` and `SUBTOTAL(3,…)` calculate only visible rows.
- Conditional formatting colours cells by rules; Excel has more built-in types (data bars, icon sets).
- For whole-row highlighting, use a custom formula with `$` before the column: `=$F2>20000000`.

## Key terms

- **Sort** — put rows in order by one or more columns.
- **Sort level** — one column in a multi-level sort.
- **Filter** — hide rows that do not meet a condition.
- **Filter view** — a saved, personal filter in Google Sheets.
- **SUBTOTAL** — a function that calculates only visible rows.
- **Conditional formatting** — formatting that is applied automatically when a rule is TRUE.
- **Applies to range** — the cells that a conditional formatting rule colours.

lessons.title: Data Validation, Protection and Print Setup
lessons.summary: You will control what people can type with dropdowns and rules, protect important cells, freeze headers, hide data and set up a sheet for printing.
goals: Create dropdown lists from a typed list and from a range
Apply number, date, text-length and custom formula validation rules
Add input messages and error alerts, and find invalid data that already exists
Freeze rows and columns and hide rows, columns and sheets
Protect a sheet so only input cells can be edited (Excel and Google Sheets)
Set a print area, print titles and fit-to-page scaling
lessons.theory:
Spreadsheets are often filled in by many people: shop assistants, accountants, teachers, managers. When people type freely, they make mistakes — a typo in a city name, 150 hours in one day, a date in the wrong year. **Data validation** stops bad data at the door, and **protection** stops people from breaking formulas by accident. In this lesson you will also learn to freeze headers, hide data and prepare a sheet for printing.

## 1. What is data validation?

**Data validation** is a rule attached to a cell or range. The rule says which values are allowed. When someone types a value that breaks the rule, the spreadsheet shows a warning or refuses the value.

Where to find it:

| Task | Microsoft Excel | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|
| Open validation | **Data > Data Validation** (Data Tools group) | **Data > Data validation** → **Add rule** |
| Keyboard | `Alt`, `A`, `V`, `V` | no default shortcut |
| Dropdown list | Allow: **List** | Criteria: **Dropdown** or **Dropdown (from a range)** |
| Custom rule | Allow: **Custom** | Criteria: **Custom formula is** |
| Rejecting bad input | Error Alert tab → Style **Stop** | Advanced options → **Reject the input** |
| Find old bad data | **Circle Invalid Data** | Invalid cells show a small **red triangle** |

## 2. Dropdown lists

A **dropdown list** lets the user pick a value from a short list instead of typing. This keeps spelling identical, so later `COUNTIF` and pivot tables work correctly.

### 2.1 Dropdown from a typed list

Excel:

1. Select the cells, for example `G2:G21`.
2. Go to **Data > Data Validation**.
3. In **Allow**, choose **List**.
4. In **Source**, type the items separated by commas: `Cash,Card,Kaspi QR`.
5. Keep **In-cell dropdown** ticked and click **OK**.

Google Sheets:

1. Select `G2:G21`, then **Data > Data validation > Add rule**.
2. In **Criteria**, choose **Dropdown**.
3. Type each item in its own box (Cash, Card, Kaspi QR). You can also choose a colour for each item.
4. Click **Done**.

### 2.2 Dropdown from a range

When the list is long or changes often, keep it on a separate sheet (for example a sheet called `Lists`) and point the rule to it.

- Excel: Allow **List**, Source `=Lists!$A$2:$A$5`.
- Sheets: Criteria **Dropdown (from a range)**, range `Lists!A2:A5`.

Now, when you add a new status to the list range, you only change the `Lists` sheet.

> **Tip:** In Excel, turn the list into a Table (`Ctrl+T`) and the dropdown can grow automatically when you add items.

## 3. Number, date and text-length rules

Not every rule is a list. You can limit numbers, dates and the length of text.

| Allow (Excel) / Criteria (Sheets) | Example rule | What it stops |
|---|---|---|
| Whole number | between 1 and 100 | 0, 250, 3.5 |
| Decimal / "Is between" | between 0 and 12 | 13 hours in a day |
| Date | between 01.10.2025 and 31.10.2025 | dates from other months |
| Text length | equal to 6 | IDs like `KZ104` or `KZ10421` |

### Worked example 1: working hours

A timesheet must have hours between 0 and 12.

| | A | B |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Name | Hours |
| 2 | Aidana Seitkali | 8 |
| 3 | Timur Bekov | 14 |
| 4 | Dana Omarova | 7.5 |

Rule on `B2:B4`: **Decimal**, **between**, minimum `0`, maximum `12`. If you add the rule after the data was typed, `B3` (14) is invalid. Excel does not delete it — you must find it. Check how many are too high with a formula:

```
=COUNTIF(B2:B4,">12")
```

Result: `1`.

> **Remember:** Validation only checks values when someone types them. Values that were already there, or values pasted over the cell, are not blocked. Use **Circle Invalid Data** (Excel) or look for red triangles (Sheets) to find them.

## 4. Custom formula validation

A **custom rule** uses a formula that must return TRUE for the value to be allowed. Write the formula for the **first cell** of the range; the spreadsheet adjusts it for the other cells, just like copying a formula.

Common custom rules:

| Goal | Formula (range starts at row 2) |
|---|---|
| No duplicate codes in `A2:A31` | `=COUNTIF($A$2:$A$31,A2)=1` |
| Discount at most 15%, unless quantity is 50 or more | `=OR(E2<=0.15,D2>=50)` |
| Text must start with "KZ" | `=LEFT(A2,2)="KZ"` |
| Date not in the future | `=C2<=TODAY()` |

### Worked example 2: no duplicate codes

| | A |
|---|---|
| 1 | Code |
| 2 | P-101 |
| 3 | P-102 |
| 4 | P-101 |

Rule on `A2:A4`: Custom, `=COUNTIF($A$2:$A$4,A2)=1`. For `A2` the formula is `COUNTIF($A$2:$A$4,A2)` = 2, so `2=1` is FALSE → invalid. `A4` is also invalid. `A3` gives 1 → valid. **Circle Invalid Data** circles 2 cells.

> **Warning:** The range in `COUNTIF` must have `$` signs (absolute), but the single cell `A2` must not. Otherwise every cell is compared with the wrong range.

## 5. Input messages and error alerts

An **input message** is a small yellow note that appears when the user selects the cell. Use it to explain the rule before the user types: "Enter hours from 0 to 12".

- Excel: **Input Message** tab → Title + Input message.
- Sheets: **Advanced options** → **Show help text for a selected cell**.

An **error alert** appears after the user types a bad value. Excel has three styles:

| Style | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Stop** | The value is refused. The user must Retry or Cancel. |
| **Warning** | "Continue?" — the user can choose Yes and keep the value. |
| **Information** | Only a message; the value is accepted. |

Google Sheets has two choices: **Show a warning** (the value stays but gets a red triangle) or **Reject the input**.

## 6. Finding invalid data

- Excel: **Data > Data Validation (arrow) > Circle Invalid Data**. Red circles appear around invalid cells. **Clear Validation Circles** removes them.
- Sheets: every cell that breaks a rule shows a red triangle in its top-right corner. Hover over it to read the reason.

You can also count invalid values with `COUNTIF` or `COUNTIFS`, which is useful for a report.

## 7. Freeze panes

When a table has 200 rows, the header disappears when you scroll. **Freezing** keeps rows or columns visible.

| Goal | Excel (View > Freeze Panes) | Google Sheets (View > Freeze) |
|---|---|---|
| Keep row 1 | **Freeze Top Row** | **1 row** |
| Keep column A | **Freeze First Column** | **1 column** |
| Keep row 1 and column A | Select `B2`, then **Freeze Panes** | **1 row** and **1 column** |

Rule in Excel: everything **above** and **to the left of** the selected cell is frozen.

## 8. Protecting sheets and ranges

### Excel: locked cells + Protect Sheet

Every cell in Excel is **Locked** by default, but "locked" does nothing until the sheet is protected.

1. Select the cells users may change (input cells).
2. Press `Ctrl+1` → **Protection** tab → untick **Locked** → OK.
3. **Review > Protect Sheet**, type a password if you want, click OK.

Now only the unlocked cells can be edited. To change other cells, use **Review > Unprotect Sheet**. **Protect Workbook** is different: it stops people adding, deleting, renaming or unhiding sheets.

### Google Sheets: Protect sheets and ranges

1. **Data > Protect sheets and ranges** (or right-click → **View more cell actions > Protect range**).
2. Choose **Range** or **Sheet**. For a sheet you can tick **Except certain cells** to leave input cells open.
3. Click **Set permissions** → **Restrict who can edit** or **Show a warning when editing**.

> **Warning:** Protection is about preventing accidents, not real security. A password-protected Excel sheet can still be copied. Never store secrets in a "protected" sheet.

## 9. Hiding rows, columns and sheets

- Hide: select the rows/columns → right-click → **Hide**. Excel shortcut: `Ctrl+9` (rows), `Ctrl+0` (columns). On Mac use `Cmd` instead of `Ctrl` for most shortcuts.
- Unhide: select the columns on both sides → right-click → **Unhide**. In Sheets, click the small arrows that appear where the columns are hidden.
- Hide a sheet: right-click the sheet tab → **Hide** (Sheets: **Hide sheet**).

Hidden cells are still used by formulas. `=SUM(I2:I121)` still adds a hidden column I.

## 10. Basic print setup

| Task | Excel | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|
| Print only part of the sheet | Select range → **Page Layout > Print Area > Set Print Area** | `Ctrl+P` → Print: **Selected cells** |
| Fit columns on one page | **Page Layout > Scale to Fit**: Width **1 page** (or `Ctrl+P` → **Fit All Columns on One Page**) | `Ctrl+P` → Scale: **Fit to width** |
| Repeat header on each page | **Page Layout > Print Titles** → Rows to repeat at top: `$1:$1` | `Ctrl+P` → **Headers & footers** → repeat frozen rows |
| Landscape | **Page Layout > Orientation** | `Ctrl+P` → Page orientation |

Use **Print Preview** (`Ctrl+P`, `Ctrl+F2` in Excel) to check before printing.

## Summary

- Data validation limits what can be typed in a cell: lists, numbers, dates, text length or a custom formula.
- Dropdowns can come from a typed list or from a range on another sheet.
- Custom rules use a formula that must return TRUE; write it for the first cell and use `$` for fixed ranges.
- Input messages explain the rule; error alerts (Stop, Warning, Information) react to bad input.
- Circle Invalid Data (Excel) and red triangles (Sheets) show values that break the rule.
- Freeze panes keep headers visible; protection stops accidental changes; hidden cells still count in formulas.
- Print area, fit to page and print titles make printed reports readable.

## Key terms

- **Data validation** — a rule that controls which values a cell accepts.
- **Dropdown list** — a list of allowed values the user can pick from.
- **Custom formula rule** — validation that allows a value only when a formula returns TRUE.
- **Input message** — help text that appears when a cell is selected.
- **Error alert** — the message shown after an invalid entry (Stop, Warning, Information).
- **Freeze panes** — keeping rows or columns visible while scrolling.
- **Locked cell** — an Excel cell that cannot be edited once the sheet is protected.
- **Protect sheet / range** — blocking edits to a whole sheet or to selected cells.
- **Print area** — the part of the sheet that will be printed.
- **Print titles** — rows or columns that repeat on every printed page.

lessons.title: Lookup Functions I: VLOOKUP, HLOOKUP and XLOOKUP
lessons.summary: You will bring prices, names and grades from one table into another with VLOOKUP, HLOOKUP and XLOOKUP, and fix the most common lookup errors.
goals: Explain what a lookup does and when you need one
Use VLOOKUP with exact match to find prices and names
Use approximate match for grades and commission brackets
Find and fix #N/A, wrong column number, extra spaces and unsorted data problems
Use HLOOKUP for horizontal tables
Use XLOOKUP with if_not_found and to return a column on the left
lessons.theory:
In real work, information is split into several tables: a price list, a list of orders, a list of employees. A **lookup** finds a value in one table and brings it into another, so you do not copy prices or names by hand. Lookup functions are among the most used skills in office jobs and are often asked about in job interviews.

## 1. Why do we need lookups?

Imagine a shop with a price list of 200 products and 5,000 orders. Each order has only a product code. To calculate the order total, you need the price of each code. Typing 5,000 prices by hand is slow and full of mistakes. A lookup function does it in one formula that you copy down.

A lookup always needs:

1. a **lookup value** — what you are searching for (for example the code `P-104`);
2. a **table** (or column) where you search;
3. the **column to return** — which information you want back (for example the price).

## 2. VLOOKUP — vertical lookup

`VLOOKUP` searches **down the first column** of a table and returns a value from the same row.

```
=VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, [range_lookup])
```

| Argument | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `lookup_value` | the value to find, e.g. `C2` |
| `table_array` | the table; the lookup value must be in its **first** column |
| `col_index_num` | which column of the table to return: 1 = first column, 2 = second … |
| `range_lookup` | `FALSE` (or `0`) = exact match; `TRUE` (or `1`, or empty) = approximate match |

### Worked example 1: price of a product (exact match)

Products (sheet `Products`, range `A1:C5`):

| | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Code | Product | Price |
| 2 | P-101 | Notebook | 450 |
| 3 | P-102 | Gel pen | 180 |
| 4 | P-103 | Backpack | 9 900 |
| 5 | P-104 | Calculator | 4 300 |

On the `Orders` sheet, `C2` contains `P-103`. Formula:

```
=VLOOKUP(C2,Products!$A$2:$C$5,3,FALSE)
```

Result: `9900`. Excel looks for `P-103` in column A of the table, goes to that row, and returns the 3rd column (Price).

> **Remember:** Lock the table with `$` signs (press `F4` after selecting it; on Mac `Cmd+T` or `Fn+F4`). Otherwise the table moves down when you copy the formula, and the lower rows return `#N/A`.

> **Tip:** Always write `FALSE` (or `0`) when you look up codes, IDs or names. Without it, VLOOKUP uses approximate match and can return a wrong value without any error.

## 3. Approximate match: brackets and grades

Approximate match (`TRUE`) is useful when you look up a value in **ranges**: grade boundaries, tax brackets, discount levels. VLOOKUP finds the **largest value that is less than or equal to** the lookup value.

The first column **must be sorted from smallest to largest**.

### Worked example 2: exam grades

| | F | G |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Min score | Grade |
| 2 | 0 | F |
| 3 | 50 | D |
| 4 | 60 | C |
| 5 | 75 | B |
| 6 | 90 | A |

Student score in `B2` = `78`.

```
=VLOOKUP(B2,$F$2:$G$6,2,TRUE)
```

Result: `B`. The largest minimum that is ≤ 78 is 75, so the grade is B. A score of 90 returns `A`, and 49 returns `F`.

### Worked example 3: commission brackets

| Sales from (₸) | Rate |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0% |
| 500 000 | 2% |
| 1 000 000 | 3.5% |
| 2 000 000 | 5% |

A manager sold 1 250 000 ₸. `VLOOKUP(1250000, table, 2, TRUE)` returns `3.5%`, so the commission is `1 250 000 × 3.5% = 43 750 ₸`.

## 4. Common VLOOKUP mistakes

| Problem | What you see | Why | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| Value not in the table | `#N/A` | the code really does not exist, or is spelled differently | check the data; later use `IFNA` (Lesson 13) |
| Extra spaces | `#N/A` | `"E105 "` is not equal to `"E105"` | use `TRIM(A2)` as lookup value, or clean the data |
| Numbers stored as text | `#N/A` | `101` (number) ≠ `"101"` (text) | convert with **Data > Text to Columns** or `VALUE()` |
| Wrong column number | wrong data (e.g. department instead of salary) | `col_index_num` counts from the **first column of the table**, not from column A of the sheet | count again |
| Column number too big | `#REF!` | the table has only 3 columns but you asked for 4 | make the table wider |
| Missing `FALSE` | wrong value, no error | approximate match on unsorted data | add `FALSE` |
| Table not locked | `#N/A` lower down | the range moved when copied | use `$A$2:$D$21` |
| Lookup column not first | `#N/A` | VLOOKUP cannot look to the left | use `XLOOKUP` or `INDEX/MATCH` |

> **Warning:** Approximate match on **unsorted** data does not always give an error. It can quietly return a wrong row. Always sort the bracket table.

## 5. HLOOKUP — horizontal lookup

`HLOOKUP` is the same idea, but the table is **horizontal**: it searches the **first row** and returns a value from a row below.

```
=HLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, row_index_num, [range_lookup])
```

| | A | B | C | D |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Month | Jan | Feb | Mar |
| 2 | Target | 400 | 420 | 450 |
| 3 | Actual | 390 | 455 | 470 |

`=HLOOKUP("Feb",$B$1:$D$3,3,FALSE)` returns `455` (row 3 of the table = Actual).

HLOOKUP is used less often, because most tables are vertical.

## 6. XLOOKUP — the modern lookup

`XLOOKUP` exists in **Excel 2021 / Microsoft 365** and in **Google Sheets**. It is not available in Excel 2016 or 2019.

```
=XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found], [match_mode], [search_mode])
```

| Argument | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `lookup_value` | what you search for |
| `lookup_array` | **one column** (or row) where you search |
| `return_array` | **one column** (or row) to return from |
| `if_not_found` | text or value to show instead of `#N/A`, e.g. `"Not found"` |
| `match_mode` | `0` exact (default), `-1` exact or next smaller, `1` exact or next larger |

Advantages over VLOOKUP:

- exact match is the **default**, so you cannot forget `FALSE`;
- no column number to count — you select the return column directly;
- it can **return from the left** of the lookup column;
- `if_not_found` replaces `#N/A` with a friendly message;
- inserting a column in the table does not break it.

### Worked example 4: returning from the left

| | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Name | Department | Employee ID |
| 2 | Aidana Seitkali | Sales | E201 |
| 3 | Timur Bekov | IT | E202 |
| 4 | Dana Omarova | Finance | E203 |

VLOOKUP cannot find a name by ID here, because the ID is in the last column. XLOOKUP can:

```
=XLOOKUP("E202",$C$2:$C$4,$A$2:$A$4,"Not found")
```

Result: `Timur Bekov`. And `=XLOOKUP("E299",$C$2:$C$4,$A$2:$A$4,"Not found")` returns `Not found`.

Grades with XLOOKUP: `=XLOOKUP(B2,$F$2:$F$6,$G$2:$G$6,,-1)` — `match_mode -1` means "exact or next smaller", the same as VLOOKUP `TRUE`.

## 7. Excel vs Google Sheets

| Feature | Excel | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|
| VLOOKUP / HLOOKUP | all versions | yes |
| XLOOKUP | Excel 2021 and Microsoft 365 only | yes |
| Lookup to another sheet | `Products!$A$2:$D$26` | same |
| Lookup to another file | open both files and click | needs `IMPORTRANGE` |
| Formula help while typing | tooltip under the formula bar | blue help box (toggle with `F1`) |
| Make reference absolute | `F4` | `F4` |

> **Tip:** When you type `=VLOOKUP(` both programs show the argument names. The bold argument is the one you are typing now. Use it to count commas.

## Summary

- A lookup finds a value in one table and returns related information from the same row (or column).
- `VLOOKUP` searches the first column; `col_index_num` counts from the first column of the table.
- Use `FALSE`/`0` for exact match (codes, IDs, names). Use `TRUE` with a **sorted** table for brackets.
- `#N/A` means "not found": check spelling, extra spaces (`TRIM`), and numbers stored as text.
- `HLOOKUP` searches the first row of a horizontal table.
- `XLOOKUP` (Excel 365/2021 and Sheets) uses separate lookup and return columns, can look left and has `if_not_found`.

## Key terms

- **Lookup value** — the value you are searching for.
- **Table array** — the range in which VLOOKUP/HLOOKUP searches.
- **Column index number** — the position of the column to return, counted from the table's first column.
- **Exact match** — find only the identical value (`FALSE` or `0`).
- **Approximate match** — find the largest value less than or equal to the lookup value (`TRUE`); needs sorted data.
- **#N/A** — the error that means the lookup value was not found.
- **XLOOKUP** — a modern lookup function with separate lookup and return arrays.
- **if_not_found** — the XLOOKUP argument that sets the result when nothing is found.

lessons.title: Lookup Functions II: INDEX, MATCH, IFERROR and IFNA
lessons.summary: You will build flexible lookups with INDEX and MATCH, find values by row and column at the same time, and replace lookup errors with clear messages.
goals: Use MATCH with match_type 0 to find the position of a value
Use INDEX to return a value by position from a column or a table
Combine INDEX and MATCH to look up values to the left or right
Build a two-way lookup with INDEX + MATCH + MATCH
Handle errors with IFNA and IFERROR
Choose between VLOOKUP, INDEX/MATCH and XLOOKUP
lessons.theory:
In Lesson 12 you used VLOOKUP and XLOOKUP. VLOOKUP has limits: it cannot look to the left, and it breaks when someone inserts a column. The pair **INDEX + MATCH** has none of these problems and works in every version of Excel and in Google Sheets. It also lets you look up a value by **row and column at the same time** — for example "sales of the Astana store in May". Finally, you will learn to replace ugly errors with clear messages using `IFERROR` and `IFNA`.

## 1. MATCH — "at which position?"

`MATCH` does not return data. It returns the **position** (a number) of a value in a list.

```
=MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_array, [match_type])
```

| Argument | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `lookup_value` | what to find |
| `lookup_array` | one row or one column |
| `match_type` | `0` = exact match (use this almost always); `1` = largest value ≤ (sorted ascending); `-1` = smallest value ≥ (sorted descending) |

### Worked example 1

| | A |
|---|---|
| 1 | City |
| 2 | Aktobe |
| 3 | Almaty |
| 4 | Astana |
| 5 | Shymkent |

`=MATCH("Astana",A2:A5,0)` → `3`. Astana is the **3rd** item of the range `A2:A5` (not row 3 of the sheet!).

`=MATCH("Taraz",A2:A5,0)` → `#N/A`, because Taraz is not in the list.

> **Warning:** If you forget the `0`, MATCH uses `1` (approximate match) and expects sorted data. For names and codes always write `0`.

MATCH is not case-sensitive: `"astana"` also finds `Astana`.

## 2. INDEX — "give me the item at this position"

`INDEX` returns the value at a given position in a range.

```
=INDEX(array, row_num, [column_num])
```

- For one column: `=INDEX(C2:C5,2)` → the 2nd value in `C2:C5`.
- For a table: `=INDEX(B2:E5,3,2)` → row 3, column 2 of the table.

### Worked example 2

| | A | B |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | City | Population (thousands) |
| 2 | Aktobe | 570 |
| 3 | Almaty | 2 230 |
| 4 | Astana | 1 420 |
| 5 | Shymkent | 1 220 |

`=INDEX(B2:B5,4)` → `1220` (the 4th value).

## 3. INDEX + MATCH together

Now combine them: MATCH finds the position, INDEX returns the value at that position.

```
=INDEX(B2:B5, MATCH("Astana", A2:A5, 0))
```

Step by step:

1. `MATCH("Astana",A2:A5,0)` → `3`
2. `INDEX(B2:B5,3)` → `1420`

Read it like a sentence: "From the Population column, give me the item at the position where Astana is in the City column."

> **Remember:** The two ranges must have the **same size and start in the same row**: `B2:B5` and `A2:A5`. If one starts at row 1 and the other at row 2, you get the wrong row.

### Looking to the left

The return column can be anywhere — left or right of the search column.

| | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Product | Price | Code |
| 2 | Notebook | 450 | ST-01 |
| 3 | Backpack | 9 900 | BG-07 |

`=INDEX(A2:A3,MATCH("BG-07",C2:C3,0))` → `Backpack`. VLOOKUP cannot do this because the code is in the last column.

### Copying the formula

When you copy the formula down, lock the ranges and leave the lookup value relative:

```
=INDEX(Catalog!$A$2:$A$41,MATCH(A2,Catalog!$D$2:$D$41,0))
```

## 4. Two-way lookup: INDEX + MATCH + MATCH

A **two-way lookup** finds the value where a **row** and a **column** cross, like finding a seat in a cinema by row and seat number.

### Worked example 3: store sales by month (million ₸)

| | A | B | C | D |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Store | Jan | Feb | Mar |
| 2 | Almaty Mega | 12.4 | 11.8 | 13.1 |
| 3 | Astana Khan | 9.6 | 10.2 | 10.9 |
| 4 | Shymkent Plaza | 7.3 | 7.9 | 8.4 |

Question: sales of **Astana Khan** in **Mar**?

```
=INDEX(B2:D4, MATCH("Astana Khan",A2:A4,0), MATCH("Mar",B1:D1,0))
```

1. Row: `MATCH("Astana Khan",A2:A4,0)` → `2`
2. Column: `MATCH("Mar",B1:D1,0)` → `3`
3. `INDEX(B2:D4,2,3)` → `10.9`

Put the store name in `G1` and the month in `G2` (maybe with dropdown lists from Lesson 11!) and use `MATCH(G1,…)` and `MATCH(G2,…)`. Now the user can change the question without touching the formula.

> **Tip:** The table in INDEX (`B2:D4`) contains **only the numbers**, without headers. The row list (`A2:A4`) must match its height, and the header list (`B1:D1`) must match its width.

## 5. Handling errors: IFERROR and IFNA

When a lookup does not find a value, it returns `#N/A`. One error also spreads: `=SUM(F2:F30)` becomes `#N/A` if one cell has an error. You can replace errors with your own value.

```
=IFERROR(value, value_if_error)
=IFNA(value, value_if_na)
```

| Function | Catches | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| `IFNA` | only `#N/A` | lookups — "not found" is expected, but other errors should stay visible |
| `IFERROR` | all errors: `#N/A`, `#DIV/0!`, `#VALUE!`, `#REF!`, `#NAME?` … | division and simple calculations |

### Worked example 4

| | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Code | Revenue | Units |
| 2 | ST-01 | 9 000 | 20 |
| 3 | XX-99 | 4 000 | 0 |

- `=IFNA(INDEX(Catalog!A:A,MATCH(A3,Catalog!C:C,0)),"Not found")` → `Not found`
- `=B3/C3` → `#DIV/0!`; `=IFERROR(B3/C3,0)` → `0`
- `=IFERROR(B2/C2,0)` → `450`

> **Warning:** Do not wrap every formula in `IFERROR` "just in case". It also hides real mistakes, such as a misspelled function name (`#NAME?`) or a deleted range (`#REF!`). For lookups, prefer `IFNA`.

## 6. Comparing VLOOKUP, INDEX/MATCH and XLOOKUP

| Feature | VLOOKUP | INDEX + MATCH | XLOOKUP |
|---|---|---|---|
| Available in | all Excel versions, Sheets | all Excel versions, Sheets | Excel 2021/365, Sheets |
| Look to the left | no | yes | yes |
| Default match | approximate (dangerous) | depends on `match_type`; write `0` | exact |
| Column number to count | yes | no | no |
| Safe when columns are inserted | no | yes | yes |
| Two-way lookup | difficult | yes (MATCH + MATCH) | yes (nested XLOOKUP) |
| Built-in "not found" | no (use IFNA) | no (use IFNA) | yes (`if_not_found`) |
| Difficulty for beginners | easy | medium | easy |

**Which one should I use?** If everyone has Microsoft 365 or Google Sheets, XLOOKUP is the easiest. If the file is used with older Excel versions, use INDEX + MATCH. VLOOKUP is fine for quick, simple tables, and you must be able to read it because many old files use it.

## 7. Excel vs Google Sheets

| Topic | Excel | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|
| INDEX, MATCH, IFERROR, IFNA | yes | yes |
| Function argument separator | `,` (some regional settings use `;`) | `,` (some locales use `;`) |
| Show formulas instead of results | `Ctrl` + grave accent key (left of `1`) | `Ctrl` + grave accent key |
| Evaluate a formula step by step | **Formulas > Evaluate Formula** | not available; select part of the formula to see a preview value |
| XMATCH (newer MATCH) | Microsoft 365 | yes |

On Mac use `Cmd` instead of `Ctrl` for most shortcuts.

> **Tip:** In Excel, select a part of a formula in the formula bar (for example the MATCH part) and press `F9` to see its result. Press `Esc` afterwards so you do not replace the formula with the number.

## Summary

- `MATCH(value, range, 0)` returns the position of a value in a row or column.
- `INDEX(range, n)` returns the n-th value; `INDEX(table, r, c)` returns the value at row r and column c.
- `INDEX(return_range, MATCH(value, search_range, 0))` is a flexible lookup that can look left.
- `INDEX(table, MATCH(row_item,…), MATCH(column_item,…))` is a two-way lookup.
- `IFNA` replaces only `#N/A`; `IFERROR` replaces every error — use it carefully.
- VLOOKUP is simple but limited; INDEX/MATCH works everywhere; XLOOKUP is the modern choice.

## Key terms

- **MATCH** — returns the position of a value in a range.
- **match_type 0** — exact match in MATCH.
- **INDEX** — returns the value at a given row (and column) position in a range.
- **Two-way lookup** — finding a value by both a row label and a column label.
- **IFERROR** — returns a chosen value when a formula gives any error.
- **IFNA** — returns a chosen value only when a formula gives #N/A.
- **#DIV/0!** — the error shown when a number is divided by zero.

lessons.title: Charts and Sparklines
lessons.summary: You will choose the right chart for your message, build and format charts in Excel and Google Sheets, and add sparklines that show trends inside cells.
goals: Choose a suitable chart type: column, bar, line, pie, combo or scatter
Create a chart in Excel and in Google Sheets from a data range
Add and edit chart elements: title, axis titles, legend and data labels
Change the chart type and data range and switch rows/columns
Create sparklines with Insert > Sparklines (Excel) and =SPARKLINE() (Sheets)
Recognise and avoid common chart mistakes
lessons.theory:
A table with 100 numbers is hard to read. A chart shows the same numbers as a picture, so a manager can see in five seconds which month was best or whether sales are growing. Charts are used in every report and presentation. In this lesson you will learn to choose the right chart, build it in Excel and Google Sheets, and avoid charts that confuse people.

## 1. Choosing the right chart

First ask: **what do I want to show?** Then choose the chart type.

| Goal | Best chart | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Compare values of a few categories | **Column chart** (vertical bars) | sales of 5 stores |
| Compare categories with long names, or many categories | **Bar chart** (horizontal bars) | 12 product names |
| Show change over time (trend) | **Line chart** | monthly visitors for 2 years |
| Show parts of a whole (one series, 2–6 parts) | **Pie chart** (or doughnut) | budget shares |
| Two measures with different units | **Combo chart** (column + line, secondary axis) | revenue in ₸ and margin in % |
| Relationship between two numbers | **Scatter chart** (XY) | hours studied vs exam score |

> **Remember:** Time goes from left to right. If the X axis is months or years, use a column or line chart — not a pie or a bar chart.

## 2. Creating a chart

The data should be a clean block: labels in the first column, a header in the first row, no empty rows.

| | A | B |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Month | Revenue (thousand ₸) |
| 2 | Jan | 820 |
| 3 | Feb | 760 |
| 4 | Mar | 905 |

### Excel

1. Select `A1:B4` (or click any cell inside the table).
2. Go to **Insert > Recommended Charts**, or choose a type in the **Charts** group (for example **Insert Column or Bar Chart > Clustered Column**).
3. Click **OK**. The chart appears on the sheet. Drag it to move it; drag a corner to resize it.

Shortcuts: `Alt+F1` creates a default chart on the same sheet; `F11` creates it on a new chart sheet. (Mac: use the Insert menu.)

### Google Sheets

1. Select `A1:B4`.
2. Go to **Insert > Chart**. Sheets guesses a chart type and opens the **Chart editor** on the right.
3. On the **Setup** tab, change **Chart type** if needed. On the **Customize** tab, change titles, colours and labels.

To open the editor again, double-click the chart (or click the three dots on the chart > **Edit chart**).

## 3. Chart elements

| Element | What it is | Excel | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Chart title** | the name of the chart | **+** (Chart Elements) button > Chart Title | Customize > Chart & axis titles |
| **Axis titles** | names of the X and Y axes, with units | + > Axis Titles | Customize > Chart & axis titles > choose axis |
| **Legend** | explains which colour is which series | + > Legend | Customize > Legend |
| **Data labels** | the value written on each column/point | + > Data Labels | Customize > Series > Data labels |
| **Gridlines** | help lines across the chart | + > Gridlines | Customize > Gridlines and ticks |

In Excel, the **+** button appears at the top-right of a selected chart. The **Chart Design** and **Format** tabs also appear on the ribbon only when a chart is selected.

> **Tip:** A good title says the message, not only the topic: "Revenue grew 18% in 2025" is better than "Revenue".

## 4. Changing the chart type and the data range

- **Change type** — Excel: **Chart Design > Change Chart Type**. Sheets: Setup > Chart type.
- **Change data** — Excel: **Chart Design > Select Data** (or drag the coloured borders around the data). Sheets: Setup > **Data range**, then add or remove series.
- **Switch rows and columns** — decides what is on the X axis and what becomes the series (the legend). Excel: **Chart Design > Switch Row/Column**. Sheets: Setup > tick **Switch rows / columns**.

### Worked example 1: switching rows and columns

| | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Month | 2024 | 2025 |
| 2 | Jan | 3 100 | 3 450 |
| 3 | Feb | 2 900 | 3 300 |
| 4 | Mar | 3 600 | 3 500 |

Default chart: months on the X axis, two series (2024 and 2025) in the legend. This compares the two years in each month. After **Switch Row/Column**: years on the X axis and three series (Jan, Feb, Mar). Usually the first version is easier to read.

In this table, 2025 is higher than 2024 in **2** months (Jan and Feb). On a line chart you see this immediately: the 2025 line is above the 2024 line, then goes below it in March.

## 5. Formatting a chart

- Click an element (a column, the axis, the title) and press `Ctrl+1` in Excel to open the **Format** pane. In Sheets use the Customize tab.
- Change colours: use one strong colour for the important series and grey for the others.
- Number format of the axis: Excel Format Axis > Number; Sheets Customize > Vertical axis > Number format.
- **Chart Styles** (Excel, Chart Design tab) give quick ready-made designs.
- Delete what you do not need: select it and press `Delete`. Fewer lines = easier to read.

### Worked example 2: data labels and the highest month

| Month | Revenue (thousand ₸) |
|---|---|
| Jan | 820 |
| Feb | 760 |
| Mar | 905 |
| Apr | 990 |

After you add data labels, the column for Apr shows **990** — the highest. You can confirm with formulas: `=MAX(B2:B5)` → `990` and `=INDEX(A2:A5,MATCH(MAX(B2:B5),B2:B5,0))` → `Apr`. The total for the four months is `=SUM(B2:B5)` → `3475`.

## 6. Pie charts and percentages

A pie chart shows each value as a share of the total. To show percentages: Excel **+ > Data Labels > More Options > Percentage**; Sheets **Customize > Pie chart > Slice label > Percentage**.

The percentage of one slice = value / total. Example: Rent 120 000 of a 300 000 ₸ budget → `=120000/300000` = **40%**.

> **Warning:** Use a pie only for **one series** with a **few parts** (up to about 6). With 12 slices nobody can compare them — use a bar chart.

## 7. Combo charts

When two series have different units (revenue in million ₸ and margin in %), one axis does not work: the % values look like 0. Use a **combo chart**:

- Excel: **Insert > Combo Chart > Custom Combination**: Revenue = Clustered Column, Margin = Line, tick **Secondary Axis** for Margin.
- Sheets: Chart type **Combo chart**; Customize > Series > choose Margin > Axis: **Right axis**.

## 8. Sparklines

A **sparkline** is a tiny chart inside one cell. It shows the trend of one row next to the numbers.

- Excel: select the empty cell (e.g. `N2`), **Insert > Sparklines > Line** (or Column, Win/Loss), Data Range `B2:M2`, OK. Copy it down with the fill handle. Use the **Sparkline** tab to mark the High Point or Low Point.
- Google Sheets: sparklines are a **function**: `=SPARKLINE(B2:M2)`. Options: `=SPARKLINE(B2:M2,{"charttype","column"})` or `{"charttype","bar"}`; colour: `{"color","green"}`.

| | Excel | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|
| Create a chart | Insert > Charts / Recommended Charts, `Alt+F1`, `F11` | Insert > Chart |
| Edit a chart | Chart Design & Format tabs, **+** button, `Ctrl+1` | Chart editor: Setup / Customize |
| Switch rows/columns | Chart Design > Switch Row/Column | Setup > Switch rows / columns |
| Sparklines | Insert > Sparklines (a feature, not a formula) | `=SPARKLINE()` function |
| Move to own sheet | Chart Design > Move Chart | three dots > Move to own sheet |
| Pivot charts | yes (Lesson 15) | any chart can use a pivot table range |

## 9. Common chart mistakes

1. **Wrong chart type** — pie for a trend over time, line for unrelated categories.
2. **No title or axis titles** — the reader does not know the units (₸? thousands? %?).
3. **Too many series** — 10 lines in one chart look like spaghetti. Show only what matters.
4. **Y axis not starting at 0 on column charts** — a small difference looks huge. Columns should start at 0.
5. **3D effects** — they make values hard to read. Use flat 2D charts.
6. **Totals included in the data** — if the table has a "Total" row, do not select it, or one giant column hides the others.
7. **Unsorted bar charts** — sort categories from largest to smallest so the order is clear.

## Summary

- Choose the chart by the message: column/bar to compare, line for trends, pie for parts of a whole, combo for two units, scatter for relationships.
- Create charts with Insert > Chart (Sheets) or Insert > Charts / `Alt+F1` (Excel).
- Add a clear title, axis titles with units, a legend when there are several series, and data labels when exact values matter.
- Use Change Chart Type, Select Data / Data range and Switch Row/Column to fix a chart without rebuilding it.
- Sparklines show a trend inside a cell: Insert > Sparklines in Excel, `=SPARKLINE()` in Sheets.
- Avoid 3D, too many slices, missing titles and including total rows.

## Key terms

- **Chart** — a visual picture of data.
- **Series** — one set of values drawn in one colour (e.g. "2025").
- **Category axis (X)** — the axis with labels such as months or names.
- **Value axis (Y)** — the axis with numbers.
- **Legend** — the key that explains series colours.
- **Data label** — the value written on a column, point or slice.
- **Combo chart** — a chart that mixes two types, often with a secondary axis.
- **Secondary axis** — a second value axis on the right for a series with different units.
- **Sparkline** — a small chart inside one cell.

lessons.theory:
A sales table with 240 rows contains many answers: which city sells the most, which product is popular in summer, which manager brings the biggest share of revenue. You could write many SUMIFS formulas — or build a **PivotTable** in one minute. PivotTables are the fastest way to summarize large data, and they are one of the most valued Excel skills in offices and banks.

## 1. What is a PivotTable?

A **PivotTable** (Google Sheets: **Pivot table**) is an interactive summary table. You choose:

- which field goes to **Rows** (for example City),
- which field goes to **Columns** (for example Quarter),
- which number goes to **Values** and how to summarize it (Sum, Count, Average…),
- which field is a **Filter** (show only one category).

The PivotTable groups the rows, does the calculations and shows a small report. The original data does not change. "Pivot" means "turn": you can turn the report around just by dragging fields.

### Worked example 1

Source data:

| Date | City | Category | Revenue |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-01-05 | Almaty | Food | 12 000 |
| 2025-01-09 | Astana | Food | 8 000 |
| 2025-02-11 | Almaty | Home | 20 000 |
| 2025-02-15 | Almaty | Food | 5 000 |
| 2025-03-02 | Astana | Home | 9 000 |

PivotTable with Rows = City, Values = Sum of Revenue:

| City | Sum of Revenue |
|---|---|
| Almaty | 37 000 |
| Astana | 17 000 |
| **Grand Total** | **54 000** |

Add Columns = Category:

| City | Food | Home | Grand Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Almaty | 17 000 | 20 000 | 37 000 |
| Astana | 8 000 | 9 000 | 17 000 |
| **Grand Total** | **25 000** | **29 000** | **54 000** |

The same result with a formula would be `=SUMIFS(D2:D6,B2:B6,"Almaty",C2:C6,"Food")` → `17000` — one formula for each cell.

## 2. Preparing the data

A PivotTable works only with a clean "flat" table:

1. **One header row**, every column has a unique name (`Date`, `City`, `Revenue`).
2. **No blank rows or columns** inside the data.
3. **No merged cells** and no subtotal rows.
4. **One type of data per column**: dates are real dates, numbers are real numbers (not text).
5. One row = one record (one order, one sale).

> **Tip:** In Excel, first turn the data into a **Table**: click inside it and press `Ctrl+T` (Mac: `Cmd+T`). When you add new rows to a Table, the PivotTable will include them after a refresh — you do not need to change the source range.

## 3. Creating a PivotTable

### Excel

1. Click any cell inside the data.
2. **Insert > PivotTable** (in some versions: **Insert > PivotTable > From Table/Range**).
3. Check the range (or table name). Choose **New Worksheet**. Click **OK**.
4. The **PivotTable Fields** pane opens on the right. Drag fields into the four areas: **Filters**, **Columns**, **Rows**, **Values**. You can also tick a field: text fields go to Rows, numbers go to Values.

### Google Sheets

1. Select the data (for example `A1:I241`).
2. **Insert > Pivot table**. Choose **New sheet**, click **Create**.
3. The **Pivot table editor** opens. Next to **Rows**, **Columns**, **Values** and **Filters** click **Add** and choose a field.

> **Remember:** Click inside the PivotTable to see the Fields pane (Excel) or the editor (Sheets). If you click outside, it disappears.

## 4. The four areas

| Area | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Rows** | one row in the report for each unique value | City: Almaty, Astana, … |
| **Columns** | one column for each unique value | Quarter: Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4 |
| **Values** | the numbers that are calculated | Sum of Revenue |
| **Filters** | show only records that match | Category = Electronics |

You can put two fields in Rows (for example City, then Salesperson) to create groups inside groups.

## 5. Summarize values by Sum, Count, Average

By default, numbers are **summed** and text is **counted**.

- Excel: click the field in Values > **Value Field Settings** > **Summarize value field by** > Sum / Count / Average / Max / Min. Or right-click a number in the pivot > **Summarize Values By**.
- Sheets: in the editor under Values > **Summarise by** > SUM / COUNTA / AVERAGE / MAX …

**Count** shows how many records (orders) there are. To count orders, put `Order ID` in Values — it becomes **Count of Order ID** (Sheets: COUNTA).

> **Warning:** If Excel shows **Count of Revenue** instead of **Sum of Revenue**, the column probably contains blank cells or text. Clean the data, or change the summary to Sum.

## 6. Sorting and formatting

- Sort: click a cell in the values column > **Data > Sort Largest to Smallest** (or right-click > **Sort**). Sheets: in Rows > **Order**: Descending, **Sort by**: SUM of Revenue.
- Number format: Excel Value Field Settings > **Number Format** (use thousands separator). Sheets: select the cells > Format > Number.
- Rename a header: just type over `Sum of Revenue` in Excel, for example `Revenue, ₸`.

## 7. Grouping dates by month and quarter

A daily date field gives too many rows. Group it:

- Excel: right-click any date in the pivot > **Group** > select **Months** and/or **Quarters** (and **Years** if the data has several years). Microsoft 365 often groups dates automatically when you drag them into Rows or Columns.
- Sheets: right-click a date in the pivot > **Create pivot date group** > **Month**, **Quarter** or **Year-Month**.

### Worked example 2

Using the data from Example 1, Rows = Date grouped by Month:

| Month | Sum of Revenue |
|---|---|
| Jan | 20 000 |
| Feb | 25 000 |
| Mar | 9 000 |

## 8. Show values as % of total

Sometimes the share is more important than the amount.

- Excel: Value Field Settings > **Show Values As** > **% of Grand Total** (also % of Column Total, % of Row Total).
- Sheets: Values > **Show as** > **% of grand total**.

In Example 1, Almaty = 37 000 / 54 000 = **68.5%**, Astana = **31.5%**.

> **Tip:** Add the same field twice to Values: once as Sum, once as % of Grand Total. Then you see both the amount and the share.

## 9. Refreshing after the data changes

A PivotTable does **not** update automatically when the source data changes.

- Excel: right-click the pivot > **Refresh**, or **PivotTable Analyze > Refresh** (`Alt+F5`; **Refresh All** = `Ctrl+Alt+F5`). If you added rows below a normal range (not a Table), use **PivotTable Analyze > Change Data Source** first.
- Sheets: pivot tables update automatically when values change. If you add rows **below** the selected range, edit the **range** at the top of the editor (or use a whole-column range such as `Sales!A:I`).

## 10. Pivot charts and slicers

- **PivotChart** (Excel): click the pivot > **PivotTable Analyze > PivotChart**. The chart follows the pivot: when you filter or change fields, the chart changes too. In Sheets, select the pivot table and use **Insert > Chart**.
- **Slicer**: a panel of buttons that filters the pivot with one click. Excel: **PivotTable Analyze > Insert Slicer** > tick City. Sheets: **Data > Add a slicer**, then choose the column. Hold `Ctrl` to choose several buttons in an Excel slicer.

## 11. Excel vs Google Sheets

| Task | Excel | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|
| Create | Insert > PivotTable | Insert > Pivot table |
| Field list | PivotTable Fields pane (drag) | Pivot table editor (Add buttons) |
| Change Sum/Count | Value Field Settings | Values > Summarise by |
| Group dates | right-click > Group | right-click > Create pivot date group |
| % of total | Show Values As | Show as |
| Refresh | Right-click > Refresh, `Alt+F5` | automatic (check the range) |
| Pivot chart | PivotChart | normal chart from the pivot range |
| Slicer | Insert Slicer | Data > Add a slicer |

## Summary

- A PivotTable summarizes a large table by grouping rows and calculating values.
- Prepare data first: one header row, no blank rows, no merged cells, correct data types.
- Rows and Columns define the groups; Values define the calculation; Filters limit the data.
- Change the calculation to Sum, Count or Average; sort the results to find the top items.
- Group dates by month or quarter; show values as % of grand total.
- Refresh in Excel after the data changes; in Sheets check that the range includes new rows.
- PivotCharts and slicers make interactive reports.

## Key terms

- **PivotTable / Pivot table** — an interactive summary table built from a data range.
- **Field** — a column of the source data (Date, City, Revenue).
- **Rows / Columns area** — where fields become row or column labels of the report.
- **Values area** — where numeric fields are summarized (Sum, Count, Average).
- **Filter** — a field that limits which records are included.
- **Grand Total** — the total of all rows or columns of the pivot.
- **Grouping** — combining dates into months, quarters or years.
- **Refresh** — recalculating the pivot from the current source data.
- **Slicer** — buttons that filter a pivot table with one click.

lessons.title: Working Together in Google Sheets: Sharing, Comments, Forms and Linked Data
lessons.summary: You will be able to share a spreadsheet safely, work on it with other people, restore old versions, collect data with Google Forms and pull data from other files and the internet.
goals: Choose the right permission (Viewer, Commenter, Editor) and share a file safely
Use comments, @mentions and assigned tasks to work with a team
Open, name and restore versions in version history

Use IMPORTRANGE, GOOGLETRANSLATE and GOOGLEFINANCE in Google Sheets
Explain the Excel equivalents: OneDrive sharing, co-authoring and Excel for the web
lessons.theory:
Today almost nobody works alone on a spreadsheet. A sales team fills one shared file, a teacher collects answers from a whole group, and a manager checks the numbers from a phone. In this lesson you learn how to work **together** on one file in Google Sheets (and in Excel Online), and how to use a few special Google Sheets functions that pull data from other places.

## 1. Sharing a file and choosing permissions

A **permission** is the right to do something with a file. In Google Sheets there are three main roles:

| Role | Can read | Can comment | Can change cells | Can share with others |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Viewer** | Yes | No | No | No |
| **Commenter** | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| **Editor** | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes (by default) |

The **owner** is the person who created the file. The owner can do everything, including deleting the file and moving ownership to someone else.

### How to share a file in Google Sheets

1. Click the green **Share** button in the top-right corner.
2. Type the email address of the person (or a Google group).
3. Choose the role on the right: **Viewer**, **Commenter** or **Editor**.
4. Keep **Notify people** ticked if you want them to get an email. You can add a short message.
5. Click **Send**.

### Link sharing

Under **General access** you can change "Restricted" to **"Anyone with the link"**. Then anyone who has the link can open the file with the role you choose (usually Viewer). This is fast, but be careful: links can be forwarded.

> **Warning:** Never give "Anyone with the link — Editor" for a file with personal data (phone numbers, salaries, marks). One wrong click by a stranger can delete your work.

> **Tip:** Follow the **principle of least privilege**: give each person the *smallest* role that lets them do their job. A director who only reads numbers needs Viewer, not Editor.

In the Share settings (the gear icon) the owner can also stop editors from changing permissions, and stop viewers and commenters from downloading, printing and copying.

## 2. Comments, @mentions and assigning tasks

A **comment** is a note attached to a cell. It does not change the cell value.

- Insert a comment: right-click a cell → **Comment**, or press `Ctrl+Alt+M` (Mac: `Cmd+Option+M`).
- A cell with a comment has a small orange triangle in the corner.
- Click **Resolve** (the tick) when the problem is fixed. Resolved comments are hidden but kept in history.

If you type `@` and an email or name inside a comment, you **mention** that person. They receive an email. You can also tick **Assign to …** — then the comment becomes a **task** (action item) for that person, and it stays open until they mark it done.

> **Remember:** Comments are for talking about the data. Notes (`Shift+F2`) are simple sticky notes without a conversation.

Example of a good comment on cell `E14`: "@arman.zhakupov@college.kz the amount 1 250 000 looks too big for one order. Please check the receipt." — then tick **Assign to Arman**.

## 3. Version history

Google Sheets saves your work automatically every few seconds. It also keeps old **versions** of the file.

1. Open **File → Version history → See version history** (`Ctrl+Alt+Shift+H`).
2. On the right you see a list of dates and times. Each person's changes have a different colour.
3. Click a version to look at it. Click **Restore this version** to go back to it.
4. To give a version a name (for example "Before cleaning" or "Final report v1"), click the three dots → **Name this version**, or use **File → Version history → Name current version**.

Restoring does not delete newer versions — they stay in the list, so you can return to them again.

You can also right-click one cell → **Show edit history** to see who changed that cell and when.

## 4. Notification rules

Go to **Tools → Notification settings → Edit notifications**. You can ask Google to send you an email when **any changes are made** or when **a user submits a form**, either right away or as a **daily digest** (one email per day). This is useful for the owner of an important shared file.

## 5. Google Forms → responses in Sheets

**Google Forms** is a free tool for surveys and quizzes. Every answer can go straight into a spreadsheet:

1. Create a form at forms.google.com and add questions.
2. Open the **Responses** tab → click **Link to Sheets** → **Create a new spreadsheet**.
3. Each new answer appears as a new row. Column A is the **Timestamp** (date and time of sending).

> **Warning:** Do not type inside the response sheet and do not sort it in place. Analyse the data on a **different sheet** with formulas, so new answers are not mixed up.

### Worked example 1: analysing form answers

| A: Timestamp | B: Name | C: Group | D: Score (1-5) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 01.10.2025 09:12 | Aidana Seitkali | 2D-1 | 5 |
| 01.10.2025 09:15 | Arman Zhakupov | 2D-2 | 3 |
| 01.10.2025 09:20 | Madina Sadykova | 2D-1 | 4 |
| 01.10.2025 09:31 | Timur Kassymov | 2D-1 | 2 |

- Number of answers: `=COUNTA(B2:B5)` → **4**
- Average score: `=AVERAGE(D2:D5)` → **3.5**
- Answers from group 2D-1: `=COUNTIF(C2:C5,"2D-1")` → **3**
- Average score of 2D-1: `=AVERAGEIF(C2:C5,"2D-1",D2:D5)` → **3.67** (11 / 3)

Using whole columns like `D:D` is a good idea for a form, because the number of rows grows: `=AVERAGE('Form Responses 1'!D:D)`.

## 6. IMPORTRANGE — data from another file

`IMPORTRANGE` copies a range from **another Google Sheets file** and keeps it updated.

```
=IMPORTRANGE("spreadsheet_url", "Sheet1!A1:E50")
```

- The first argument is the URL (or the long ID) of the other file, in quotes.
- The second argument is the sheet name and range, in quotes.
- The first time, you see `#REF!` with the button **Allow access**. Click it to connect the two files.
- You need at least **Viewer** access to the source file.

You can put IMPORTRANGE inside other functions:

```
=SUM(IMPORTRANGE("https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1AbC.../edit", "Sales!E2:E41"))
```

## 7. GOOGLETRANSLATE and GOOGLEFINANCE

These functions work **only in Google Sheets** and need the internet.

`=GOOGLETRANSLATE(text, source_language, target_language)` translates text. Language codes: `"en"` English, `"ru"` Russian, `"kk"` Kazakh. Use `"auto"` to detect the source language.

### Worked example 2: translation and currency

| A | B (formula) | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Keyboard | `=GOOGLETRANSLATE(A2,"en","ru")` | Клавиатура |
| 100 (USD) | `=A3*GOOGLEFINANCE("CURRENCY:USDKZT")` | about 51 000 (depends on today's rate) |

`GOOGLEFINANCE("CURRENCY:USDKZT")` returns the current exchange rate of 1 US dollar in tenge. Other pairs: `"CURRENCY:EURKZT"`, `"CURRENCY:RUBKZT"`. The rate can be delayed by up to 20 minutes and is only for information, not for official accounting.

> **Tip:** Put the rate in **one cell** (for example `H1`) and refer to it with an absolute reference `$H$1` in all formulas. Then you change the rate only in one place.

## 8. Offline mode

Without internet you can still edit Google Sheets in Chrome:
1. Install the **Google Docs Offline** extension.
2. In Google Drive go to **Settings → Offline** and tick the box.
3. In the file use **File → Make available offline**.
When you are online again, your changes are synchronised. Functions like GOOGLEFINANCE do not update offline.

## 9. Excel vs Google Sheets: working together

| Task | Google Sheets | Excel (Microsoft 365) |
|---|---|---|
| Where the file lives | Google Drive | OneDrive or SharePoint |
| Share | **Share** button → Viewer / Commenter / Editor | **Share** button → "Can edit" / "Can view" (and "Can review" in some versions) |
| Work at the same time | Always (real-time) | **Co-authoring** when the file is saved on OneDrive; you see colored cursors of others |
| Browser version | Sheets is always in the browser | **Excel for the web** (Excel Online), free with a Microsoft account |
| Comments and @mentions | Yes, with "Assign to" | Yes, threaded comments with @mentions; "Assign" in Microsoft 365 |
| Version history | File → Version history | File → Info → **Version History** |
| Forms | Google Forms → Link to Sheets | **Microsoft Forms** → Open results in Excel |
| Link to another file | `IMPORTRANGE` | External reference like `='[Sales.xlsx]Sheet1'!A1` or Power Query |
| Translate / currency | `GOOGLETRANSLATE`, `GOOGLEFINANCE` | Review → **Translate**; Data → **Currencies** data type |

> **Remember:** In Excel, co-authoring works only when the file is saved in the cloud (OneDrive/SharePoint) and **AutoSave** is on. A file on your desktop cannot be edited by two people at once.

## Summary

- Share with the smallest role that is enough: Viewer (read), Commenter (read + comment), Editor (change).
- Link sharing is quick but risky for private data.
- Comments with @mentions send an email; "Assign to" turns a comment into a task.
- Version history lets you see, name and restore older versions without losing newer ones.
- Google Forms can send every answer into a Sheet; analyse it on a separate sheet.
- `IMPORTRANGE` reads data from another Google Sheets file after you click Allow access.
- `GOOGLETRANSLATE` and `GOOGLEFINANCE("CURRENCY:USDKZT")` are Sheets-only internet functions.
- Excel uses OneDrive, co-authoring and Excel for the web for the same ideas.

## Key terms

- **Permission (role)** — what a person is allowed to do with a file: view, comment or edit.
- **Owner** — the person who created the file and controls it fully.
- **Link sharing** — access for anyone who has the file link.
- **Comment** — a message attached to a cell; can mention and assign people.
- **@mention** — typing @ and a name/email so that person is notified.
- **Version history** — the list of saved older states of a file.
- **Named version** — a saved version you gave a clear name.
- **IMPORTRANGE** — a Sheets function that imports a range from another file.
- **GOOGLEFINANCE** — a Sheets function that returns market data such as exchange rates.
- **Co-authoring** — several people editing one Excel file at the same time (in OneDrive/SharePoint).

lessons.title: Dynamic Arrays and Power Functions: FILTER, SORT, UNIQUE, QUERY
lessons.summary: You will be able to filter, sort and summarise data with single formulas that spill results, and ask questions of data with QUERY in Google Sheets.
goals: Explain what a spill range is and fix #SPILL! errors
Use UNIQUE and COUNTA(UNIQUE()) to list and count distinct values
Filter data with FILTER using one condition, AND conditions and OR conditions
Sort with SORT and SORTBY (Excel) and multi-column SORT (Sheets), and create numbers with SEQUENCE
Write simple QUERY formulas with SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, ORDER BY and LIMIT in Google Sheets
lessons.theory:
Until now, one formula gave one answer in one cell. **Dynamic array** functions are different: one formula can return a whole list or table. With them you can filter, sort and remove duplicates with a single formula that updates by itself when the data changes. Analysts in banks, shops and offices use these functions every day because they save a lot of time.

## 1. What is a spill range?

When a formula returns many values, the values **spill** into the cells below and to the right. The area they fill is the **spill range**. You type the formula only in the first cell.

| A | B (formula in B2) |
|---|---|
| Almaty | `=UNIQUE(A2:A7)` → Almaty |
| Astana | Astana |
| Almaty | Shymkent |
| Shymkent | |
| Astana | |
| Almaty | |

In Excel the spill range has a thin blue border. You can edit the formula only in the first cell (B2); the other cells are grey "ghost" values.

> **Warning:** If something is already typed in the cells where the result wants to spill, you get the `#SPILL!` error in Excel or `#REF!` ("Array result was not expanded…") in Google Sheets. Clear the blocking cells and the result appears.

> **Remember:** `FILTER`, `SORT`, `SORTBY`, `UNIQUE` and `SEQUENCE` work in **Excel 365 and Excel 2021 or newer**, and in all versions of Google Sheets. In Excel 2016/2019 they show `#NAME?`.

To refer to a whole spill range, write the first cell with `#`: `=COUNTA(B2#)` counts all spilled values (Excel only).

## 2. UNIQUE — remove duplicates with a formula

`=UNIQUE(range)` returns each value only once.

- `=UNIQUE(D2:D91)` — list of all cities without repeats.
- `=COUNTA(UNIQUE(D2:D91))` — **how many** different cities there are.
- `=SORT(UNIQUE(D2:D91))` — the unique list in A→Z order.

## 3. FILTER — keep only the rows you want

```
=FILTER(array, include, [if_empty])
```

- **array** — the data to return (one column or the whole table).
- **include** — a condition that gives TRUE/FALSE for each row, for example `D2:D91="Almaty"`.
- **if_empty** — what to show if nothing matches, for example `"No orders"`.

### Worked example 1: FILTER with one and two conditions

| A: Customer | B: City | C: Total |
|---|---|---|
| Aidana | Almaty | 12 000 |
| Arman | Astana | 55 000 |
| Dana | Almaty | 61 000 |
| Timur | Almaty | 8 000 |

- One condition: `=FILTER(A2:C5, B2:B5="Almaty")` → 3 rows (Aidana, Dana, Timur).
- Two conditions with **AND** — multiply them: `=FILTER(A2:A5, (B2:B5="Almaty")*(C2:C5>50000))` → **Dana**.
- Two conditions with **OR** — add them: `=FILTER(A2:A5, (B2:B5="Astana")+(C2:C5>60000))` → Arman, Dana.
- Sum of the filtered values: `=SUM(FILTER(C2:C5, B2:B5="Almaty"))` → **81 000**.

Why multiply? TRUE counts as 1 and FALSE as 0. 1×1 = 1 only when **both** are true. In an addition the result is at least 1 when **any** of them is true.

> **Tip:** In Google Sheets you can also write several conditions separated by commas: `=FILTER(A2:C5, B2:B5="Almaty", C2:C5>50000)` — this means AND. Excel does not allow this form; use `*`.

## 4. SORT and SORTBY

```
=SORT(array, [sort_index], [sort_order], [by_col])
```

- **sort_index** — which column of the array to sort by (1, 2, 3 …).
- **sort_order** — `1` ascending (A→Z, small→large), `-1` descending in Excel. In Google Sheets it is `TRUE` for ascending and `FALSE` for descending.

Examples (data A2:C5 above):
- Excel: `=SORT(A2:C5, 3, -1)` — sort by Total, largest first.
- Google Sheets: `=SORT(A2:C5, 3, FALSE)`.

**Several sort columns:**
- Excel: `=SORT(A2:C5, {2,3}, {1,-1})` — by City A→Z, then by Total from large to small. Or use **SORTBY**, which sorts by any range, even one that is not shown in the result:
  `=SORTBY(A2:A5, B2:B5, 1, C2:C5, -1)`.
- Google Sheets: `=SORT(A2:C5, 2, TRUE, 3, FALSE)` — pairs of (column, order). Sheets has no SORTBY, but its SORT can take a range instead of a column number: `=SORT(A2:A5, C2:C5, FALSE)`.

**Top N.** Combine with other functions: Excel `=TAKE(SORT(A2:C91,3,-1),5)` or Sheets `=ARRAY_CONSTRAIN(SORT(A2:C91,3,FALSE),5,3)` show the 5 largest rows.

## 5. SEQUENCE — a list of numbers

`=SEQUENCE(rows, [columns], [start], [step])`

- `=SEQUENCE(5)` → 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (down a column).
- `=SEQUENCE(1,12)` → 1 … 12 across a row (month numbers).
- `=SEQUENCE(4,1,100,50)` → 100, 150, 200, 250.

Use it to number rows of a filtered list: `=SEQUENCE(COUNTA(F2#))` in Excel.

## 6. ARRAYFORMULA (Google Sheets)

In Google Sheets, a normal formula like `=G2*H2` calculates one row. `ARRAYFORMULA` makes it work on whole ranges at once:

```
=ARRAYFORMULA(G2:G91*H2:H91)
```

One formula in `I2` fills the whole column. Shortcut: type the formula and press `Ctrl+Shift+Enter` — Sheets wraps it in ARRAYFORMULA for you. In Excel 365 you do not need it: `=G2:G91*H2:H91` spills automatically.

## 7. QUERY — SQL-like questions in Google Sheets

`QUERY` is a **Google Sheets only** function. It uses a small language similar to SQL (the language of databases):

```
=QUERY(data, "query text", [headers])
```

Columns are named by their letters: `A`, `B`, `C`… (inside the data range). The parts must be written in this order:

| Clause | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `SELECT` | which columns to show | `SELECT C, I` |
| `WHERE` | which rows to keep | `WHERE D = 'Almaty' AND I > 50000` |
| `GROUP BY` | make groups and summarise | `SELECT F, SUM(I) GROUP BY F` |
| `ORDER BY` | sort the result | `ORDER BY I DESC` |
| `LIMIT` | show only the first N rows | `LIMIT 5` |

Text in the query is in **single quotes** (`'Almaty'`), the whole query is in double quotes.

### Worked example 2: QUERY

Data in `A1:I91` (headers in row 1): Order ID, Date, Customer, City, Product, Category, Qty, Price, Total.

- Top 3 orders: `=QUERY(A1:I91, "SELECT A, C, I ORDER BY I DESC LIMIT 3", 1)`
- Revenue by category: `=QUERY(A1:I91, "SELECT F, SUM(I) GROUP BY F ORDER BY SUM(I) DESC", 1)` → a small table, the first row is the best category.
- Orders from Almaty with total over 50 000: `=QUERY(A1:I91, "SELECT * WHERE D = 'Almaty' AND I > 50000", 1)`
- Number of orders by city: `=QUERY(A1:I91, "SELECT D, COUNT(A) GROUP BY D", 1)`

The last argument `1` says the data has 1 header row. Other aggregate functions: `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `COUNT`.

> **Tip:** In Excel there is no QUERY. Use FILTER + SORT, a PivotTable, or **Power Query** (Data → Get & Transform) for similar results.

## 8. Excel vs Google Sheets

| Function / feature | Excel 365 / 2021+ | Google Sheets |
|---|---|---|
| Spill error | `#SPILL!` | `#REF!` (array result was not expanded) |
| FILTER, UNIQUE, SEQUENCE | Yes | Yes |
| FILTER with AND | `(cond1)*(cond2)` | `(cond1)*(cond2)` or `cond1, cond2` |
| SORT descending | `-1` | `FALSE` |
| SORT by several columns | `SORT(..., {2,3}, {1,-1})` or `SORTBY` | `SORT(range, 2, TRUE, 3, FALSE)` |
| ARRAYFORMULA | Not needed (spills by itself) | Needed for normal formulas on ranges |
| QUERY | No (use Power Query / PivotTable) | Yes |
| Refer to a spill range | `F2#` | Use the full range, e.g. `F2:F` |

## Summary

- Dynamic array formulas return many values that spill into nearby cells; keep those cells empty.
- `UNIQUE` removes repeats; `COUNTA(UNIQUE(...))` counts distinct values.
- `FILTER` keeps rows that match; use `*` for AND and `+` for OR.
- `SORT`/`SORTBY` sort with a formula; Excel uses 1/-1, Sheets uses TRUE/FALSE.
- `SEQUENCE` makes lists of numbers; `ARRAYFORMULA` makes Sheets formulas work on whole columns.
- `QUERY` (Sheets only) uses SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, ORDER BY, LIMIT in that order.
- These functions need Excel 365 or Excel 2021+.

## Key terms

- **Dynamic array** — a formula result that contains many values.
- **Spill range** — the cells filled by a dynamic array formula.
- **#SPILL!** — Excel error when the spill range is blocked.
- **FILTER** — returns only rows that meet a condition.
- **UNIQUE** — returns each value once.
- **SORTBY** — Excel function that sorts one range by the values in another range.
- **SEQUENCE** — creates a list of numbers.
- **ARRAYFORMULA** — Sheets function that applies a formula to whole ranges.
- **QUERY** — Sheets function that asks questions of data with an SQL-like language.

lessons.title: Data Cleaning: Tables, Duplicates, Splitting and Fixing Messy Data
lessons.summary: You will be able to turn messy, inconsistent data into clean data that gives correct totals and counts.
goals: Explain why dirty data gives wrong results and list typical data problems
Create an Excel Table and write formulas with structured references
Clean text with TRIM, CLEAN and PROPER and convert numbers stored as text with VALUE
Split combined fields with Text to Columns, Split text to columns and SPLIT
